      How images work (lazy evaluation)

      An Image is a recipe, not pixels in memory.

      Operation Pixels read
      raster.image(), raster.mosaic(), raster.stack(), split(), select(), rename(), addBands(), band math, comparisons, normalizedDifference(), expression(), where(), remap(), clip(), updateMask(), cluster(), pca(), geometry(), bounds(), bandNames(), meta(), print(img) None
      sample() Only the blocks that contain sampled pixels
      visualize() A downsampled preview (longest side ≤ max_size, default 1500 px)
      save() The full image, streamed in 1024 × 1024 blocks
      img.data The full image, all at once

      You can chain as many operations as you like at no cost. Pixels are read only at the end, and only as much as needed. See Memory and performance.

      raster.image(path)

      Opens a raster and returns an Image. Only the metadata is read.

      Parameter Type Description
      path str or Path Path to a GeoTIFF, or any format rasterio can read. Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory when the image is created.

      Returns: Image

      Raises: - RasterNotFoundError if path does not exist or is not a file. - RasterReadError if the file exists but rasterio cannot open it.

      img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif")
print(img)
# <Image sampleImage1.tif bands=['B1', 'B2', ..., 'MSK_CLASSI_SNOW_ICE'] shape=(26, 551, 763)>

      The file must stay in place while the Image is in use, because pixels are read from it on demand.

      Image attributes

      Attribute Type Description
      path str The path the image was loaded from. Derived images keep the original path.
      res tuple[float, float] Pixel size (x, y) in CRS units.
      data numpy.ndarray (float32) All pixels at full resolution, shape (bands, rows, cols). Computed each time it is accessed. Store it in a variable if you need it more than once. NoData pixels are NaN. 
      img.path                        # 'sampleImage1.tif'
img.res                         # (8.983152841195215e-05, 8.983152841195215e-05)

arr = img.select("B8").data     # compute once, keep the array
arr.shape                       # (1, 551, 763)
float(np.nanmean(arr))          # average NIR value

      The extent is available as img.bounds().

      Image.bandNames()

      Returns the band names in band order, as a BandList.

      A BandList is an ordinary Python list (indexing, len(), in and loops all work) with two extras:

      Method Returns
      .size() Number of bands (int)
      .get(i) Band name at 0-based index i 
      img.bandNames()              # ['B1', 'B2', 'B3', 'B4', ...]
img.bandNames().size()       # 26
img.bandNames().get(0)       # 'B1'
"B8" in img.bandNames()      # True

      Names come from the band descriptions in the GeoTIFF. A band with no description is named B<n>, where n is its 1-based band number.

      Image.select(*bands)

      Selects bands, returning a new Image with only those bands, in the order given. No pixels are read or copied.

      Parameter Type Description
      *bands str, int, or one list/tuple of them Band names or 1-based band numbers. See Specifying bands.

      Raises: ValueError if no bands are given, or a band does not exist.

      nir = img.select("B8")
rgb = img.select("B4", "B3", "B2")
rgb = img.select(["B4", "B3", "B2"])
fcc = img.select([8, 4, 3])

      Image.rename(*names)

      Renames the bands, returning a new Image.

      Parameter Type Description
      *names str, or one list of str One name per band.

      Raises: ValueError if the number of names doesn't match the number of bands.

      ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI")
rg = img.select("B4", "B3").rename(["red", "green"])

      Image.addBands(other)

      Adds the bands of other after this image's bands, returning a new Image.

      Raises: - TypeError if other is not an Image. - ValueError if the images are on different pixel grids, or if band names would be duplicated. Use rename() first.

      ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI")
stack = img.select("B4", "B8").addBands(ndvi)
stack.bandNames()          # ['B4', 'B8', 'NDVI']
stack.save("stack.tif")

      To combine more than two images, or images on different grids, use raster.stack().

      Image.split(save=False)

      Splits the image into single-band images, one per band, in band order. No pixels are read unless you save.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      save bool or str False True also saves each band as its own GeoTIFF, named <image>_<band>.tif, in the current folder. A string saves them into that folder, which is created if needed.

      Returns: list of Image, one per band.

      Raises: TypeError if save is not True, False or a folder path.

      bands = img.split()
bands[3].bandNames()                        # ['B4']
for band in img.select("B2", "B3", "B4").split():
    band.visualize(palette="gray")

img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8").split(save="bands/")
# bands/sampleImage1_B2.tif, bands/sampleImage1_B3.tif, bands/sampleImage1_B4.tif, bands/sampleImage1_B8.tif

      Saved files keep the integer type of the source when it has one, and each file stores its band name.

      raster.stack(images, names=None, save=False)

      Stacks the bands of several images into one multi-band image, for example single-band files (one GeoTIFF per band) or a mix of bands and computed indices. Nothing is read until you visualize or save.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      images list, folder, or pattern – A list of Images and/or file paths; a folder (all .tif/.tiff files, in name order); or a glob pattern such as "bands/*_B0[2348].tif". All must have the same CRS.
      names list of str – New band names, one per band of the result.
      save bool or str False True saves stack_stack_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path.

      Returns: Image with the bands of all inputs, in order.

      Raises: ValueError if no images are given, the CRSs differ, or names has the wrong length.

      s = raster.stack(["B02.tif", "B03.tif", "B04.tif", "B08.tif"],
                 names=["blue", "green", "red", "nir"])
s = raster.stack("bands/")                                    # every .tif in a folder
s = raster.stack([img.select("B8"), ndvi.rename("NDVI")], save="nir_ndvi.tif")
      • The first image sets the grid (extent and pixel size). Images on a different grid are resampled to it with nearest neighbour; areas they don't cover become NoData. For example, Sentinel-2 20 m bands stacked after a 10 m band are resampled to 10 m.
      • Band names: the original names are kept. Where names repeat, which is common with single-band files whose band is always called B1, they are prefixed with the file name, e.g. T43_B04_B1. Pass names= to choose your own.
      • Split and stack are opposites: raster.stack(img.split()) gives back the same image.

      Image.bounds(save=False)

      Returns the image's bounding box. It can also save the box as a GeoJSON rectangle.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      save bool or str False True saves the box to <image>_bounds_<epoch>.geojson in the current folder. A string saves to that path: GeoJSON for .geojson/.json, and other vector formats such as .shp or .kml also work.

      Returns: BoundingBox(left, bottom, right, top) in the image's CRS. Read the values as b.left, b.bottom, b.right, b.top.

      Raises: TypeError if save is not True, False or a file path.

      extent = evi.bounds()
# BoundingBox(left=73.0923..., bottom=33.6800..., right=73.1608..., top=33.7295...)
extent.left, extent.top

extent = evi.bounds(save=True)                    # also writes sampleImage1_bounds_1795578943.geojson
extent = evi.bounds(save="evi_extent.geojson")    # choose the file name

      GeoJSON is always written in EPSG:4326 (longitude/latitude), so an image in UTM gets a GeoJSON in degrees. After clip(), the bounds are those of the clipped image.

      bounds() is always the axis-aligned rectangle. geometry() follows the image's actual corners and returns a Vector you can inspect further. For normal north-up images, both give the same rectangle.

      Image.geometry()

      Returns the image's extent (footprint) as a Vector containing one polygon, in the image's CRS. Print it, inspect it, or export it.

      extent = img.geometry()
print(extent)
# <Vector sampleImage1 (extent) | 1 feature | Polygon | EPSG:4326>
#            name                                                     geometry
# 0  sampleImage1  POLYGON ((73.09232 33.72958, 73.16086 33.72958, 73.16086 ...

extent.meta()
extent.toGeoJSON()                      # GeoJSON dict
extent.save("extent.geojson")           # or .shp, .kml, .gpkg, .csv, ...

      The polygon follows the image's actual corners, so it is correct for rotated images too. After clip(), it is the extent of the clipped image.

      Image.clip(geometry, save=False)

      Clips the image to a vector: 1. Crops the image to the vector's bounding box. The result is smaller, faster, and uses less memory. 2. Masks every pixel outside the shapes, so those pixels become NoData (NaN).

      The vector is reprojected to the image's CRS automatically. A pixel counts as inside when its center is inside a shape, which is the same rule GDAL and rasterio.mask use.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      geometry Vector – e.g. vector.Open("boundary.shp"), or another image's .geometry(). All features are used.
      save bool or str False True saves <image>_clip_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path.

      Returns: Image (lazy, like everything else)

      Raises: - TypeError if geometry is not a Vector. - ValueError if the vector is a table without geometries, has no CRS, or doesn't overlap the image.

      from earthforge import raster, vector

img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif")
aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")

clipped = img.clip(aoi)
clipped.select("B4", "B3", "B2").visualize(min=1000, max=4000, gamma=1.2)

# Clip any result, and save in one step
img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI").clip(aoi, save="ndvi_aoi.tif")

      A clipped image has a different size from the original, so it can only be combined in band math with images clipped the same way.

      Image.updateMask(mask, save=False)

      Masks the image: wherever mask is 0 or NoData, pixels become NoData. Any non-zero value keeps the pixel. Use it to keep only some classes, or only pixels that meet a condition.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      mask Image – 1 band (applied to every band) or the same number of bands as the image.
      save bool or str False True saves <image>_updateMask_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path. 
      # True color, only where the class map says "dense vegetation" (class 4)
img.select("B4", "B3", "B2").updateMask(classified.eq(4)).visualize(min=1000, max=4000)

# NDVI without water
ndvi.updateMask(ndvi.gt(0))

      Image.sample()

      Image.sample(numPixels=5000, seed=0, geometries=True, progress=True, region=None)

      Samples random pixels and returns their band values as a vector dataset, one row per pixel. It is used to train clusterers and PCA, and it's handy for statistics, charts or exporting training data.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      numPixels int 5000 Number of random pixels.
      seed int 0 Random seed: the same seed gives the same pixels.
      geometries bool True Add a point at each pixel centre. False gives a plain table.
      progress bool True Show a progress bar on large images.
      region Vector – Only sample pixels whose centre is inside these shapes. Reprojected to the image's CRS automatically. The full numPixels are drawn inside the region when it has that many pixels.

      Returns: Vector with one column per band.

      Raises: ValueError if numPixels is not a positive whole number, or the region doesn't overlap the image; TypeError if region isn't a Vector.

      Pixels with NoData in any band are left out, so the result can have fewer rows than requested.

      samples = img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8").sample(2000)
samples.show(5)
samples.data.describe()                          # statistics with pandas
samples.save("training_pixels.csv")

ndvi_samples = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI").sample(1000)

aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
inside = img.sample(1000, region=aoi)            # 1000 pixels, all inside the boundary

# or a geometry you define yourself (see vector: Creating your own geometries)
img.sample(1000, region=vector.Rectangle(73.11, 33.69, 73.14, 33.71))
img.sample(300, region=vector.Point(73.125, 33.700).buffer(500))     # within 500 m of a point

      What is read. Sampling reads as little as possible:

      • Samples spread thinly over a large image (e.g. 5,000 pixels on a huge mosaic): only the small 256 × 256 tiles that hold a sample are read, and only the sampled pixels are computed. Memory stays at a few MB.
      • Dense samples (many samples per block, or a small image): whole 1024 × 1024 blocks are read, which is faster when most of the image would be touched anyway.

      The library chooses automatically, and the result is identical either way. On a 30,000 × 30,000 raster (2.9 GB), 2,000 samples took 2.2 s with 1 MB of memory, against 3.1–5.6 s and about 110 MB when reading whole blocks. On images too big for the computer's file cache, the difference is much larger.

      Image.cluster() and Image.pca()

      Method Returns
      img.cluster(clusterer, outputName="cluster", numPixels=5000, seed=0, region=None) A lazy single-band image of cluster numbers (0, 1, 2, ...). Give a trained clusterer, or an untrained one to train it on this image (inside region if given). Saved as uint8 with NoData = 255.
      img.pca(model, numPixels=10000, standardize=False, seed=0, region=None) A lazy image with bands PC1, PC2, ..., from a trained PCA or a number of components (trained inside region if given). 
      from earthforge import cluster, pca

trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)
img.cluster(trained).visualize(labels={i: f"Cluster {i}" for i in range(5)})
img.cluster(cluster.wekaKMeans(5), region=aoi)        # train inside aoi and apply, in one step

pcs = img.pca(pca.PCA(3).train(img))
pcs.visualize(bands=["PC1", "PC2", "PC3"])
img.pca(3, region=aoi)                                # same idea for PCA

      See Clustering and PCA for all methods and options.

      Image.meta()

      Prints a summary of the image and returns its metadata. Reads no pixels.

      Returns: dict with driver, dtype, nodata, width, height, count, crs, transform, bandNames.

      For images produced by band math, the header says (computed), dtype is float32, and nodata is nan. That matches what save() writes.

      img.select("B4", "B3", "B2").meta()

      =============================================
 Metadata for: sampleImage1.tif
=============================================
 Driver     : GTiff
 Width      : 763 px
 Height     : 551 px
 Bands      : 3
 Band names : ['B4', 'B3', 'B2']
 Data type  : float64
 NoData     : None
 CRS        : EPSG:4326
 Resolution : (8.983152841195215e-05, 8.983152841195215e-05)
 Bounds     : BoundingBox(left=73.0923..., bottom=33.6800..., right=73.1608..., top=33.7295...)
 Transform  :
| 0.00, 0.00, 73.09|
| 0.00,-0.00, 33.73|
| 0.00, 0.00, 1.00|
=============================================

      In Jupyter, write img.meta(), not print(img.meta()). Otherwise the returned dict is printed as well.

      Image.save()

      Image.save(path=None, compress="deflate", dtype=None, nodata=None, progress=True, workers=None)

      Writes the image to a GeoTIFF. The image is computed and written in 1024 × 1024 pixel blocks, so memory use depends on the block size, not on the image size. On a computer with several CPU cores, blocks are computed in parallel. A progress bar shows how far it is: a widget in Jupyter, a text bar in a terminal.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      path str auto Output file. The default is <image stem>_<band names>_<unix epoch>.tif in the current working directory.
      compress str or None "deflate" "deflate" (small, widely supported), "zstd" (a little faster), "lzw" (faster, larger file), or None (fastest, largest file).
      dtype str auto Data type of the file, e.g. "uint16", "int16", "float32". Auto: the source's integer type when pixel values pass through unchanged (select, clip, updateMask, "first"/"last"/"min"/"max" mosaics), otherwise float32. Computed values saved to an integer type are rounded and clipped to the type's range.
      nodata number auto Value written for NoData pixels. Auto: NaN for float types; for integer types the source's NoData value, or 0.
      progress bool True Show a progress bar.
      workers int auto How many blocks are computed at the same time. Auto: one per CPU core, up to 8 (raster.MAX_WORKERS), and fewer if the blocks in progress would need more than about a quarter of the free memory. 1 processes one block at a time. See Memory and performance.

      Returns: the absolute path of the written file (str).

      Raises: ValueError if path is one of the files the image reads from, dtype is unknown, nodata doesn't fit in an integer dtype, or workers is less than 1.

      Output format: - band names stored as band descriptions, so raster.image() reads them back - tiled 256×256 (for images at least 256 px in each direction), with a predictor suited to the data type and multi-threaded compression - BigTIFF used automatically when the file would exceed 4 GB

      img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI").save("ndvi.tif")      # float32
img.select("B4", "B3", "B2").save()                 # keeps the file's type if it is an integer type
(img * 0.0001).save("reflectance.tif", compress="zstd")
classified.save("classes.tif", dtype="uint8", nodata=255)                    # small class map

      Band-math methods also accept a save argument that calls save() for you. See Band math.

      Image.visualize(...)

      Image.visualize(bands=None, min=None, max=None, gamma=1.0, palette=None,
                colorbar=True, colorbar_label=None, colorbar_orientation="vertical",
                labels=None, overlay=None, overlay_color="red", max_size=1500,
                save_chart=False, dpi=200)

      Displays the image as a map chart with matplotlib. Each band is stretched linearly from min to max, then gamma correction is applied. It can show an RGB composite (3 bands), a single band with a palette and colorbar, or a class map with a legend.

      Only a downsampled preview is read: its longest side is at most max_size pixels. The axes show map coordinates (latitude/longitude for geographic CRSs, otherwise X/Y), and the stretch values are printed below the chart.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      bands str, int, list, or Image first 3 bands (first band if fewer than 3) 1 band for a single-band view, 3 bands for an RGB composite in [red, green, blue] order. If you pass an Image (for example bands=img.select("B8")), that image is shown.
      min float or list[float] 2nd percentile of each band Value mapped to the lowest color. One number for all bands, or one per band.
      max float or list[float] 98th percentile of each band Value mapped to the highest color.
      gamma float or list[float] 1.0 output = stretched1/gamma. Above 1 brightens, below 1 darkens.
      palette str or list "gray" Single band only. A built-in palette, a matplotlib colormap, or a list of colors. See Palettes.
      colorbar bool True Single band only. Shows a colorbar labeled with real pixel values.
      colorbar_label str band name Colorbar title.
      colorbar_orientation "vertical" or "horizontal" "vertical" Colorbar placement: right of the map, or below it.
      labels dict None Single band only. For class maps: {value: "name"}. Draws flat colors with a legend instead of a colorbar. See Showing class maps.
      overlay Vector or list None Vectors drawn on top of the image: polygons as outlines, lines as lines, points as dots. They are reprojected to the image's CRS, and the map keeps the image's extent. See Drawing vectors on an image.
      overlay_color str or list "red" Color of the overlay; a list gives one color per overlay vector.
      max_size int 1500 Longest side of the preview, in pixels. Higher shows more detail but uses more memory. Images smaller than this are shown at full resolution.
      save_chart bool False Also saves the chart as PNG in the current working directory, named <image stem>_<unix epoch>.png.
      dpi int 200 Resolution of the saved PNG. Ignored unless save_chart=True.

      Returns: the saved file name (str) if save_chart=True, otherwise None.

      Raises: ValueError when: - bands has a number of bands other than 1 or 3, - a band does not exist, - min, max or gamma is a list whose length doesn't match the number of bands, - palette is used with 3 bands, - palette is unknown or contains an invalid color, - colorbar_orientation is invalid, - labels is not a non-empty dict, is used with 3 bands, or its number of classes doesn't match a palette list.

      Raises: TypeError if bands is a list that contains an Image.

      Examples

      # RGB composites
img.visualize(bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], min=1000, max=4000, gamma=1.2)      # true color
img.visualize(bands=["B8", "B4", "B3"], min=0, max=[5000, 4000, 4000])      # false color

# Indices
img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI").visualize(min=-0.2, max=0.8, palette="ndvi")
img.normalizedDifference(["B3", "B8"]).rename("NDWI").visualize(
    min=-0.6, max=0.4, palette="ndwi", colorbar_orientation="horizontal")

# Single bands
img.select("B8").visualize(palette="viridis")
img.visualize(bands=img.select("B8"), min=250, max=2500)       # an Image works as `bands` too
img.select("B8").visualize(palette=["0000FF", "FFFFFF", "008000"], min=1000, max=5000)

# Class map with a legend (see Reclassify)
classes.visualize(labels={1: "Water", 2: "Sparse", 3: "Moderate", 4: "Dense"},
                  palette=["0000FF", "D2B48C", "9ACD32", "006400"])

# A boundary (or any vector) drawn on top
img.visualize(bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], overlay=vector.Open("boundary.shp"), overlay_color="yellow")

# Save at high resolution
img.visualize(bands=[4, 3, 2], save_chart=True, dpi=300)
      True color NDVI (palette="ndvi") NDWI, horizontal colorbar

      NoData

      Pixels equal to the source file's NoData value, and NaN results of band math (such as division by zero), are excluded from the percentile stretch and drawn transparent.

      Scripts and Jupyter

      • In a script, plt.show() blocks until the chart window is closed.
      • The PNG is saved before the chart is shown, so save_chart=True works in both.
      • Each figure is closed after it is shown, so repeated calls don't accumulate memory.

      Specifying bands

      Wherever a method takes bands (select, visualize, normalizedDifference), each band can be the following. Inside expression(), use band names or b() instead, where b(i) is 0-based.

      Form Example Meaning
      Name "B8A" Matches an entry in bandNames() exactly (case-sensitive).
      Number 9 1-based band number, the same numbering as rasterio and GDAL.

      Names and numbers can be mixed: img.select("B4", 3, "B2").

      Limitations

      • Clipped images have their own grid: a clipped image can be combined only with images clipped the same way, not with the original full image.
      • Source files must stay in place: pixels are read on demand, so moving or deleting the source file breaks images derived from it.
      • img.data loads everything: it computes the full image in memory. Prefer visualize() or save() for large images. See Memory and performance.
      • Computation is float32: pixels are converted to float32 when read, even if the file stores float64. That's about 7 significant digits, plenty for imagery and indices.
      • meta() transform display: values are shown to 2 decimal places, so very small pixel sizes show as 0.00. The Resolution line and the returned transform hold the full values.
      • Default stretch: when min/max are omitted, a 2–98 percentile stretch is used per band. For consistent colors across images, pass min/max explicitly.
      • Preview resampling: visualize() downsamples with nearest-neighbour, so thin features may disappear in previews of very large images. Raise max_size to see them.
      PreviousHomeNextBand math

      User guide

      Band math

      Arithmetic between images and numbers, band by band. Every operation returns a new lazy Image. Nothing is computed until you visualize(), save() or access .data.

      from earthforge import raster
img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif")

nir, red = img.select("B8"), img.select("B4")
ratio = nir.divide(red)                       # method style
ratio = nir / red                             # operator style, same result
ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"])

      For text formulas, see Expressions. For reclassification, see Reclassify with where().

      • Methods
      • Operators
      • Comparisons and logic
      • normalizedDifference(bandNames=None, save=False)
      • Rules for combining images
      • The save argument
      • Invalid results become NaN
      • Recipes

      Methods

      Binary: image.op(other, save=False)

      other can be an Image or a number (int, float or NumPy scalar).

      Method Computes
      add(other) image + other
      subtract(other) image - other
      multiply(other) image * other
      divide(other) image / other (division by 0 → NaN)
      pow(other) image ** other

      Unary: image.op(save=False)

      Method Computes
      abs() absolute value
      sqrt() square root (negative → NaN)
      log() natural log (≤ 0 → NaN)
      log10() base-10 log (≤ 0 → NaN)
      exp() ex 
      nir, red = img.select("B8"), img.select("B4")

total = nir.add(red)                   # nir + red
diff = nir.subtract(red)               # nir - red
scaled = nir.multiply(0.0001)          # nir * 0.0001
ratio = nir.divide(red)                # nir / red
squared = nir.pow(2)                   # nir ** 2

magnitude = diff.abs()                 # abs(diff)
root = nir.sqrt()
log_ratio = ratio.log()
db = ratio.log10() * 10                # decibels
back = log_ratio.exp()                 # undoes log()

diff = nir.subtract(red, save="diff.tif")    # any of them can save directly

      Raises: - TypeError if other is neither an Image nor a number. - ValueError if the images are on different grids or have incompatible band counts. See Rules.

      Operators

      Python operators work as shorthand for the methods above. They have no save argument; call .save() on the result instead.

      Expression Same as
      a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b, a ** b a.add(b), a.subtract(b), a.multiply(b), a.divide(b), a.pow(b)
      2 * a, 1 - a, 1 / a, 2 ** a the number can be on either side
      -a a.multiply(-1)
      abs(a) a.abs() 
      evi = 2.5 * (nir - red) / (nir + 6 * red - 7.5 * blue + 1)

      Comparisons and logic

      These return images of 1 (true) and 0 (false), and NaN where an input is NoData. Use them as masks, or as tests in where(). Every method also takes save=False.

      Method Operator 1 where…
      lt(other) a < other a < other
      lte(other) a <= other a ≤ other
      gt(other) a > other a > other
      gte(other) a >= other a ≥ other
      eq(other) – a = other (a list: a equals any of them)
      neq(other) – a ≠ other (a list: a equals none of them)
      And(other) a & other both non-zero
      Or(other) a \| other either non-zero
      Not() ~a a is zero 
      ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"])
moderate = ndvi.gt(0.34).And(ndvi.lt(0.5))       # method style
moderate = (ndvi > 0.34) & (ndvi < 0.5)          # operator style, same result
not_water = ndvi.lt(0).Not()                     # or ~ndvi.lt(0)
extreme = ndvi.lt(0).Or(ndvi.gt(0.8))            # or (ndvi < 0) | (ndvi > 0.8)
land = classified.neq([0, 1])                    # neither class 0 nor class 1
fraction = moderate.data.mean()                  # share of pixels that are moderate
      • And / Or / Not are capitalized because and / or / not are Python keywords (.and() is a SyntaxError). The lowercase spellings and_(), or_() and not_() work too. Using and / or / if on an image raises a TypeError that explains this.
      • == and != are deliberately not overloaded, so images keep working as dict keys and in lists. Use .eq() / .neq().
      • With operators, add parentheses around each comparison, because & binds more tightly than >.

      normalizedDifference(bandNames=None, save=False)

      Calculates the Normalized Difference between two bands: (first − second) / (first + second) for every pixel. Pixels where the sum is 0 become NaN.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      bandNames list of 2 band names or numbers first two bands The two bands, in order.
      save bool or str False See The save argument. Auto file name: <image>_nd_<epoch>.tif.

      Returns: a single-band Image named "nd", with values from −1 to 1. Rename it with .rename().

      Raises: ValueError if bandNames doesn't contain exactly 2 bands, or the image has fewer than 2 bands.

      Index Call (Sentinel-2) Suggested palette
      NDVI (vegetation) normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]) "ndvi"
      NDWI (water, McFeeters) normalizedDifference(["B3", "B8"]) "ndwi"
      MNDWI (water) normalizedDifference(["B3", "B11"]) "water"
      NDBI (built-up) normalizedDifference(["B11", "B8"]) "ndbi"
      NBR (burn) normalizedDifference(["B8", "B12"]) "nbr"
      NDSI (snow) normalizedDifference(["B3", "B11"]) "ndsi"

      Rules for combining images

      When both operands are images:

      1. Same pixel grid. Width, height, CRS and transform must match, or a ValueError is raised. Bands from the same file always match.
      2. Band pairing.
      3. Same number of bands: paired in order (band 1 with band 1, and so on).
      4. One image has 1 band: that band is used against every band of the other.
      5. Anything else: ValueError.
      6. Output band names come from the left operand. When the left image has 1 band and the right has several, the right image's names are used.
      img.select("B4", "B3", "B2") / img.select("B8")     # 3 bands: B4/B8, B3/B8, B2/B8 → names ['B4','B3','B2']
img.select("B4", "B3") + img.select("B8", "B2")     # 2 bands, paired in order
img.select("B4", "B3") + img.select("B8", "B2", "B1")   # ValueError

      A number is applied to every band: img * 0.0001 scales all 26 bands.

      The save argument

      Every band-math method (add, subtract, multiply, divide, pow, abs, sqrt, log, log10, exp, the comparison and logic methods, normalizedDifference, expression, where) has a save argument:

      Value Effect
      False (default) Nothing is written.
      True Saves to <image stem>_<operation>_<unix epoch>.tif in the current working directory.
      "path.tif" Saves to that path.

      The method always returns the resulting Image, so you can keep chaining or visualize it:

      ratio = img.select("B8").divide(img.select("B4"), save=True)
# Saved: C:\...\sampleImage1_divide_1795498682.tif  (1 band(s), float32)
ratio.visualize(palette="viridis")

img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"], save="ndvi.tif")

      save= uses Image.save() with its defaults. To choose a compression or rename the bands first, call .save() yourself:

      img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI").save("ndvi.tif", compress="zstd")

      Invalid results become NaN

      Results that are not finite are set to NaN. NaN pixels are drawn transparent and saved as NoData. This covers: - division by zero, - log of values ≤ 0, sqrt of negative values, - overflow to ±infinity.

      NoData pixels in the source file also become NaN when read, so they stay NoData through any calculation.

      All calculations run in float32.

      Recipes

      img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif")
blue, green, red, nir, swir1 = (img.select(b) for b in ["B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11"])

# Scale Sentinel-2 L2A digital numbers to reflectance
refl = img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8").multiply(0.0001)

# EVI
evi = (2.5 * (nir - red) / (nir + 6 * red - 7.5 * blue + 1)).rename("EVI")

# SAVI (L = 0.5)
savi = ((nir - red) / (nir + red + 0.5) * 1.5).rename("SAVI")

# Simple ratio, saved directly
sr = nir.divide(red, save="simple_ratio.tif")

# Stack of indices in one file
stack = (img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI")
            .addBands(img.normalizedDifference(["B3", "B8"]).rename("NDWI"))
            .addBands(img.normalizedDifference(["B11", "B8"]).rename("NDBI")))
stack.save("indices.tif")

      For EVI and SAVI, scale the bands to reflectance (0–1) first. The constants in those formulas assume reflectance values.

      PreviousImagesNextExpressions

      User guide

      Expressions

      Image.expression() evaluates a formula written as text. It is often easier to read than chained band-math calls.

      evi = img.expression(
    "2.5 * ((NIR - RED) / (NIR + 6 * RED - 7.5 * BLUE + 1))",
    {
        "NIR": img.select("B8").multiply(0.0001),
        "RED": img.select("B4").multiply(0.0001),
        "BLUE": img.select("B2").multiply(0.0001),
    },
).rename("EVI")

      The result is a normal lazy Image: chain more operations on it, visualize() it, or save() it.

      Safe by design

      The formula is parsed into a syntax tree and only the operations listed below are allowed. It is never run as Python code, so something like __import__("os") is rejected.

      Signature

      Image.expression(expression, map=None, save=False)
Image.Expression(...)      # alias, same function
      Parameter Type Default Description
      expression str – The formula.
      map dict None Variable name → Image or number.
      save bool or str False True saves <image>_expression_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path.

      Returns: Image. Band names follow the band-math rules (the left-most image's names), so use .rename() to name the result.

      What you can write

      Syntax Example Notes
      Variables from map NIR, RED Images must be on the same pixel grid. Numbers are also allowed.
      Band names B8, B4 This image's bands can be used directly, without a map.
      b('name') b('B8') Band by name.
      b(index) b(7) Band by 0-based index (b(0) is the first band).
      Numbers 2.5, 1e-4
      Arithmetic + - * / ** ** is power. Unary - works too.
      Parentheses ( … )
      Comparisons < <= > >= == != Give 1 (true) or 0 (false). Chains like 0.2 < x < 0.5 work.
      Logic, symbols && \|\| !
      Logic, Python style and or not
      Functions abs(), sqrt(), log(), log10(), exp()

      Not supported: the ternary cond ? a : b, %, and other functions. For if/else logic use where().

      Examples

      # NDVI from band names directly
ndvi = img.expression("(B8 - B4) / (B8 + B4)").rename("NDVI")

# Same with b()
ndvi = img.expression("(b('B8') - b('B4')) / (b('B8') + b('B4'))")

# SAVI with a constant passed in the map
savi = img.expression(
    "((NIR - RED) / (NIR + RED + L)) * (1 + L)",
    {"NIR": img.select("B8") * 0.0001, "RED": img.select("B4") * 0.0001, "L": 0.5},
).rename("SAVI")

# Water mask: 1 where green > NIR and NIR is low
water = img.expression("B3 > B8 && B8 < 1500").rename("water")
water.visualize(palette=["white", "blue"], min=0, max=1)

# Values within a range
mid = img.expression("1000 < B8 < 2000")

# Images from different variables, saved directly
img.expression("sqrt(abs(NIR - RED))", {"NIR": img.select("B8"), "RED": img.select("B4")},
               save="diff.tif")

      Errors

      Message Cause
      Unknown name 'FOO' in expression. Add it to the map, … The name is neither in map nor a band name.
      Invalid expression 'B8 +': invalid syntax The formula can't be parsed.
      Unsupported syntax in expression: '…' It uses something not in the table above.
      The expression must use at least one band or image. Something like "1 + 2", which has no image in it.
      b(99): band index must be 0..25 (0-based) The index is out of range.
      map value for 'X' must be an Image or a number, got str A map value has the wrong type.
      PreviousBand mathNextReclassify & classes

      User guide

      Reclassify with where() and remap()

      • Image.where() reclassifies a raster: wherever a condition is true, the pixel value is replaced. Give one rule, or several at once. Use it for ranges, for example NDVI 0.3–0.43 → class 2.
      • Image.remap() replaces exact values with new values. Use it to recode or merge classes, for example classes 1 and 2 → 1.
      • eq(), selectClasses(), mergeClasses() pick or combine classes in a class map.
      ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI")

classes = ndvi.where(
    (ndvi.lt(0.1), 1),                          # water / bare
    (ndvi.gte(0.1).And(ndvi.lt(0.34)), 2),      # sparse vegetation
    (ndvi.gte(0.34).And(ndvi.lt(0.5)), 3),      # moderate vegetation
    (ndvi.gte(0.5), 4),                         # dense vegetation
    otherwise=0,
).rename("class")

classes.visualize(
    labels={1: "Water / bare", 2: "Sparse vegetation", 3: "Moderate vegetation", 4: "Dense vegetation"},
    palette=["0000FF", "D2B48C", "9ACD32", "006400"],
    colorbar_label="NDVI class",
)
classes.save("ndvi_classes.tif")

      Signature

      Image.where(*rules, otherwise=None, save=False)
      Parameter Type Default Description
      *rules (test, value) pairs – test is an Image (a condition). Where it is non-zero, the pixel becomes value (a number or an Image). See Rule formats.
      otherwise number None Value for pixels that match no rule. None keeps the original value.
      save bool or str False True saves <image>_where_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path.

      Returns: Image with the same band names as the input.

      How rules are applied

      1. Start from the original image, or from otherwise if it is given.
      2. Apply the rules in order. Where a rule's test is true (non-zero), that rule's value is written.
      3. Where rules overlap, the last matching rule wins. This is the same as chaining several .where() calls.
      4. Where a test is NoData (NaN), the pixel is not changed by that rule.

      Rule formats

      All of these give the same result:

      ndvi.where((ndvi.lt(0.1), 1), (ndvi.gte(0.5), 2), otherwise=0)

      ndvi.where(ndvi.lt(0.1), 1)
# chain for several rules:
ndvi.where(ndvi.lt(0.1), 1).where(ndvi.gte(0.5), 2)

      rules = [(ndvi.lt(0.1), 1), (ndvi.gte(0.5), 2)]
ndvi.where(rules, otherwise=0)

      ndvi.where({ndvi.lt(0.1): 1, ndvi.gte(0.5): 2}, otherwise=0)


      ndvi.where({ndvi.lt(0.1), 1}, {ndvi.gte(0.5), 2}, otherwise=0)
      Python sets have no order. This form works only when the value is a number: the Image is taken as the test and the number as the value. Use tuples when the value is an image.

      Building conditions

      Conditions are images of 1 (true) and 0 (false), made with comparisons and logic:

      Method Operator Meaning
      x.lt(v) x < v less than
      x.lte(v) x <= v less than or equal
      x.gt(v) x > v greater than
      x.gte(v) x >= v greater than or equal
      x.eq(v) – equal
      x.neq(v) – not equal
      a.And(b) a & b both true
      a.Or(b) a \| b either true
      a.Not() ~a not true

      and / or / not don't work on images

      and, or and not are Python keywords. That means:

      • ndvi.gt(0.2).and(ndvi.lte(0.3)) is a SyntaxError. Python rejects it before the code runs.
      • ndvi.gt(0) and ndvi.lt(1) raises a TypeError that explains what to use instead.

      Use one of these, which all give the same result:

      Style AND OR NOT
      Capitalized a.And(b) a.Or(b) a.Not()
      Lowercase a.and_(b) a.or_(b) a.not_()
      Operators a & b a \| b ~a

      With operators, use parentheses: (ndvi > 0.34) & (ndvi < 0.5). In Python, & binds more tightly than >.

      Use otherwise for a clean class map

      Without otherwise, pixels that match no rule keep their original value. NDVI values below your lowest class would then stay in the result as -0.59, 0.05 and so on. Add otherwise=0 (or any other value) so every pixel gets a class.

      Range rules

      Classes that cover ranges of values are written as two comparisons joined with And:

      reclassified = ndvi.where(
    (ndvi.gt(0.2).And(ndvi.lte(0.3)), 1),
    (ndvi.gt(0.3).And(ndvi.lte(0.43)), 2),
    (ndvi.gt(0.43).And(ndvi.lte(0.62)), 3),
    (ndvi.gt(0.62), 4),
    otherwise=0,
)

      Each rule is a pair (condition, value), so check the brackets: the condition's And(...) closes before the comma and the class value.

      More examples

      # Clip negative NDVI to 0, leave everything else unchanged
ndvi.where(ndvi.lt(0), 0)

# Replace values using another image: fill NoData in B8 with B8A
img.select("B8").where(img.select("B8").eq(0), img.select("B8A"))

# Binary mask: 1 = vegetation, 0 = everything else
veg = ndvi.where(ndvi.gte(0.3), 1, otherwise=0)

# Rules built from an expression
water = img.expression("B3 > B8 && B8 < 1500")
landcover = ndvi.where((ndvi.gte(0.4), 2), (water, 1), otherwise=0)

# Reclassify and save in one step
ndvi.where((ndvi.lt(0.2), 1), (ndvi.gte(0.2), 2), otherwise=0, save="veg_classes.tif")

      Picking and merging classes

      Once you have a class map (for example classified from the examples above), these methods pick or combine classes:

      Task Code Result
      Pick one class as a mask classified.eq(3) 1 where class 3, 0 elsewhere
      Pick several classes as a mask classified.eq([3, 4]) 1 where class 3 or 4, 0 elsewhere
      Everything except some classes classified.neq([0, 1]) 1 where the class is neither 0 nor 1
      Keep only some classes classified.selectClasses([3, 4]) class values 3 and 4 kept, all others NoData
      Merge classes classified.mergeClasses([1, 2], into=1) classes 1 and 2 become 1, others unchanged
      Several merges at once classified.mergeClasses({1: [1, 2], 2: [3, 4]}) 1, 2 → 1 and 3, 4 → 2
      Imagery for one class only img.updateMask(classified.eq(4)) image pixels only where class 4 
      # Area share of dense vegetation (class 4)
share = classified.eq(4).data.mean()

# Show only the vegetation classes
classified.selectClasses([3, 4]).visualize(labels={3: "Moderate", 4: "Dense"},
                                           palette=["6BBF3A", "006400"])

# Merge 5 classes into 3, then save
classified.mergeClasses({0: [0], 1: [1, 2], 2: [3, 4]}, save="ndvi_3classes.tif")

      eq(value) / neq(value)

      value can be a number, an Image, or a list of numbers. With a list, eq gives 1 where the pixel equals any of the values, and neq gives 1 where it equals none of them. NoData stays NoData.

      selectClasses(classes, save=False)

      Keeps the listed class values and turns every other pixel into NoData. classes is one number or a list.

      mergeClasses(classes, into=None, save=False)

      Parameter Type Description
      classes list of numbers, or dict The classes to merge into into. Or a dict {new_value: [old_values]} for several merges at once (then leave out into).
      into number The value the merged classes get. Required unless classes is a dict.
      save bool or str True saves <image>_mergeClasses_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path.

      Classes not listed keep their value. A class can't be listed in two groups.

      Remap values with remap()

      Image.remap() replaces specific values with new values. Use it to recode a class map, for example to merge classes or convert codes from one scheme to another. where() works with conditions such as ranges; remap() works with exact values.

      # 5 NDVI classes (0-4) -> 3 classes
merged = classes.remap([0, 1, 2, 3, 4], [0, 1, 1, 2, 2])

# Same, as a dict {old: new}
merged = classes.remap({0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 2, 4: 2})

merged.visualize(labels={0: "Non-vegetation", 1: "Sparse", 2: "Dense"},
                 palette=["D3D3D3", "C8E66E", "006400"])

      Signature

      Image.remap(from_values, to_values=None, default=None, save=False)
      Parameter Type Default Description
      from_values list of numbers, or dict – The values to replace. Or a dict {old: new}, in which case leave out to_values.
      to_values list of numbers None The new values, one per entry in from_values.
      default number None Value for pixels whose value isn't listed. None keeps their original value. Use float("nan") to make them NoData.
      save bool or str False True saves <image>_remap_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path.

      Returns: Image with the same band names. It applies to every band, and NoData stays NoData.

      Raises: ValueError if the lists are empty, have different lengths, or contain something other than numbers. TypeError if default is not a number.

      How values are matched

      • Values are matched exactly, so remap() is meant for class or integer values. For continuous data such as NDVI, use where() with ranges.
      • Every value is matched against the original pixel values. With remap([1, 2], [2, 3]), pixels that were 1 become 2 and pixels that were 2 become 3. A 1 is never turned into 3.

      More examples

      # Binary mask: classes 3 and 4 -> 1, everything else -> 0
veg = classes.remap([3, 4], [1, 1], default=0)

# Keep only water (class 1); everything else becomes NoData
water_only = classes.remap([1], [1], default=float("nan"))

# Recode and save in one step
classes.remap({1: 10, 2: 20, 3: 30, 4: 40}, save="recoded.tif")

      Showing class maps

      Pass labels to visualize() to get flat colors and a legend instead of a continuous colorbar:

      Argument Description
      labels {value: "name"} for each class to show. Pixels with other values are transparent.
      palette A list with one color per class (in order of value), or a palette name to sample from (default "tab10").
      colorbar_label Legend title (default: the band name).

      min, max and gamma are ignored when labels is given.

      PreviousExpressionsNextClustering

      User guide

      Clustering

      Clustering (unsupervised classification) groups pixels or table rows with similar values, without training labels. You choose a method, train it on a sample, and apply it to an image or a dataset.

      from earthforge import raster, cluster

img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif").select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11", "B12")

trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(5, init="kmeans++", restarts=3).train(img, numPixels=5000)
trained.info()                                   # sizes and centres of the clusters

clusters = img.cluster(trained)                  # lazy: one band named "cluster" (0, 1, 2, ...)
clusters.visualize(labels={i: f"Cluster {i}" for i in range(5)})
clusters.save("clusters.tif")                    # streamed block by block; uint8, NoData = 255

      Water (cluster 2) and the bright roads and buildings (cluster 1) stand out clearly. The cluster numbers themselves have no meaning: compare trained.centers() with what you know about the area to name them.

      • The three steps
      • Methods
      • Training: train()
      • Training inside a region
      • Applying: img.cluster() and vector.cluster()
      • Inspecting a trained clusterer
      • Choosing the number of clusters
      • Clustering tables
      • Memory and speed
      • Tips

      The three steps

      Step Code What happens
      1. Choose a method c = cluster.wekaKMeans(5) Nothing is computed yet.
      2. Train trained = c.train(img, numPixels=5000) A random sample of pixels is read and the clusters are learned from it.
      3. Apply img.cluster(trained) / table.cluster(trained) Every pixel or row gets the number of its nearest cluster. Images stay lazy.

      Steps 2 and 3 can also be done in one call: img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5), region=aoi).

      Training on a sample keeps it fast and light on memory. A few thousand pixels are usually enough to find the main groups.

      Methods

      All methods are created by a function in cluster. All of them have a normalize option, which scales every input to 0–1 before clustering so that inputs with large values (e.g. B8 near 3000) don't outweigh small ones.

      Function Groups by Chooses the number of clusters normalize default
      cluster.kMeans(nClusters) nearest centre (k-means++ start, several restarts) no False
      cluster.wekaKMeans(nClusters, init, distanceFunction) nearest centre; options in the style of Weka's SimpleKMeans no True
      cluster.wekaCascadeKMeans(minClusters, maxClusters) nearest centre yes, best Calinski–Harabasz score True
      cluster.wekaXMeans(minClusters, maxClusters) nearest centre yes, best BIC True
      cluster.miniBatchKMeans(nClusters) nearest centre, trained on small batches: fast for large samples no False
      cluster.bisectingKMeans(nClusters) splits the largest cluster in two until there are nClusters no False
      cluster.gaussianMixture(nClusters, covariance) most likely of nClusters Gaussian groups; clusters can be stretched, not just round no False

      cluster.kMeans(nClusters, maxIterations=300, restarts=4, normalize=False)

      Standard k-means. Every pixel goes to the nearest of nClusters centres, and each centre is the mean of its pixels.

      trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)
trained = cluster.kMeans(5, normalize=True, restarts=10).train(img)

      cluster.wekaKMeans(nClusters, init="random", distanceFunction="Euclidean", maxIterations=500, restarts=1, normalize=True)

      k-means with the options of Weka's SimpleKMeans:

      Parameter Options
      init "random": random samples as first centres. "kmeans++": spread-out centres, picked by probability. "farthestFirst": each next centre is the sample farthest from those chosen so far.
      distanceFunction "Euclidean" (straight-line distance; centres are means) or "Manhattan" (sum of differences; centres are medians, which is less sensitive to outliers).
      restarts Runs with different starts; the one with the lowest total distance is kept.
      normalize True by default, as in Weka. 
      trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(5).train(img)
trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(6, init="kmeans++", distanceFunction="Manhattan", restarts=5).train(img)
trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(4, init="farthestFirst").train(img)

      cluster.wekaCascadeKMeans(minClusters=2, maxClusters=10, restarts=10, init="random", maxIterations=500, normalize=True)

      Tries every number of clusters from minClusters to maxClusters and keeps the one with the best Calinski–Harabasz score (clusters that are compact and far apart), in the style of Weka's CascadeSimpleKMeans.

      trained = cluster.wekaCascadeKMeans(2, 8).train(img, numPixels=5000)
trained.nClusters          # the number it chose
trained.info()             # the score for every number tried

      cluster.wekaXMeans(minClusters=2, maxClusters=8, restarts=3, init="kmeans++", maxIterations=500, normalize=True)

      Like the cascade, but chooses the number of clusters with the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), which rewards a good fit and penalizes extra clusters (the X-means idea of Pelleg and Moore, as in Weka's XMeans).

      trained = cluster.wekaXMeans(2, 10).train(img, numPixels=5000)

      cluster.miniBatchKMeans(nClusters, batchSize=1024, maxIterations=100, normalize=False)

      A faster k-means that updates the centres from small random batches. Use it to train on large samples (50,000+ pixels).

      trained = cluster.miniBatchKMeans(6).train(img, numPixels=50000)

      cluster.bisectingKMeans(nClusters, normalize=False)

      Starts with one cluster and keeps splitting the largest one in two. The clusters tend to be more even in size.

      trained = cluster.bisectingKMeans(5).train(img)

      cluster.gaussianMixture(nClusters, covariance="full", normalize=False)

      Models the data as a mix of Gaussian (bell-shaped) groups. covariance sets their shape: "full" (any shape), "diag" (aligned with the axes), "spherical" (round) or "tied" (all the same shape).

      trained = cluster.gaussianMixture(5).train(img)
trained = cluster.gaussianMixture(4, covariance="diag").train(img)

      On data with 4 clearly separated groups, every method finds them exactly (adjusted Rand index 1.0 in our tests), and the cascade and X-means both choose 4 clusters on their own.

      Training: train()

      Clusterer.train(data, inputProperties=None, numPixels=5000, seed=0, region=None)
      Parameter Type Default Description
      data Image or Vector – Image: numPixels random pixels are sampled with img.sample(). Vector (a table, a CSV, or img.sample() output): its numeric columns are used.
      inputProperties list of str all The bands or columns to learn from. Default: all bands, or all numeric columns.
      numPixels int 5000 Pixels to sample from an image.
      seed int 0 Random seed for the sample and the clustering: the same seed gives the same result.
      region Vector – Train only on pixels (or rows) inside these shapes, e.g. your study area. The trained clusterer can still be applied to the whole image.

      Returns: a TrainedClusterer.

      Raises: ValueError if there are fewer valid samples than clusters, or a column is missing or not numeric; TypeError if data isn't an Image or a Vector, or region isn't a Vector.

      Pixels or rows with NoData in any input are left out of training.

      trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=10000, seed=1)
trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, inputProperties=["B4", "B8", "B11"])   # some bands only

samples = img.sample(5000)                      # or train on a sample you keep
trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(samples)

aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, region=aoi)          # learn inside the boundary only
img.cluster(trained)                                         # ...and apply everywhere

      Training inside a region

      Pass region= (any vector: a boundary, a district, a field) to learn the clusters from that area only. Every training pixel is drawn inside the shapes, and you still get the full numPixels. Regions in another CRS are reprojected automatically.

      from earthforge import vector

districts = vector.Open("sample_data/districts.geojson")
central = districts.filter(vector.Filter.eq("district", "Central"))

# two steps: train inside the region, then apply
trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(4, restarts=3).train(img, region=central, numPixels=3000)
trained.centers()
img.cluster(trained)                         # the whole image, with clusters learned in Central
img.clip(central).cluster(trained)           # or just the region

# one step: train inside the region and apply
clusters = img.cluster(cluster.wekaKMeans(4, restarts=3), region=central, numPixels=3000)

      Both forms give the same result. The clusters describe the land covers of the region. In the Central district, which is mostly lake, 69% of the training pixels fall into one cluster with very low NIR (B8) and SWIR (B11, B12) values, which is water. The other three split the shore, vegetation and built-up areas more finely than clusters learned on the whole image would.

      Use Code
      Train inside a region, apply to the whole image img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, region=aoi))
      Train inside a region, keep only the region img.clip(aoi).cluster(cluster.kMeans(5), region=aoi)
      Train on the whole image, show only the region img.clip(aoi).cluster(cluster.kMeans(5).train(img))

      Sampling with your own geometry

      The region can be any geometry you define yourself. No file is needed (see Creating your own geometries):

      from earthforge import vector

# a rectangle from coordinates (longitude, latitude)
box = vector.Rectangle(73.11, 33.69, 73.14, 33.71)
trained = cluster.kMeans(4).train(img, region=box)
trained.info()

# a polygon from its corners
lake = vector.Polygon([(73.110, 33.690), (73.145, 33.692), (73.148, 33.716), (73.118, 33.712)])
clusters = img.cluster(cluster.wekaKMeans(4), region=lake)       # train inside the polygon and apply

# a circle of 500 m around a point
circle = vector.Point(73.125, 33.700).buffer(500)
trained = cluster.gaussianMixture(3).train(img, region=circle, numPixels=2000)

# a shape drawn on geojson.io (paste the GeoJSON), or WKT text
drawn = vector.fromGeometry({"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[73.11, 33.69], [73.14, 33.69],
                                                                 [73.14, 33.71], [73.11, 33.69]]]})
wkt = vector.fromGeometry("POLYGON ((73.11 33.69, 73.14 33.69, 73.14 33.71, 73.11 33.69))")
trained = cluster.wekaCascadeKMeans(2, 6).train(img, region=drawn)

# coordinates in another CRS (UTM metres): reprojected automatically
box_utm = vector.Rectangle(323500, 3729500, 326500, 3731500, crs="EPSG:32643")
trained = cluster.kMeans(4).train(img, region=box_utm)

# several training areas at once, e.g. one per land cover you care about
from shapely.geometry import box as shape_box
areas = vector.fromGeometry([shape_box(73.10, 33.70, 73.11, 33.71), shape_box(73.15, 33.68, 73.16, 33.69)],
                            properties={"name": ["urban sample", "farm sample"]})
trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, region=areas)             # pixels from both areas

      You can also sample first and keep the sample, for example to inspect or save it, then train on it:

      samples = img.sample(5000, region=lake)         # 5,000 pixels, all inside the polygon
samples.show(5)
samples.visualize()                             # where the samples are
samples.save("training_pixels.geojson")
trained = cluster.kMeans(4).train(samples)

      All numPixels are drawn inside the geometry, as long as it covers that many pixels.

      Applying: img.cluster() and vector.cluster()

      Image.cluster(clusterer, outputName="cluster", numPixels=5000, seed=0, region=None)

      Assigns every pixel to a cluster. The result is a lazy single-band image of cluster numbers (0, 1, 2, ...), so you can visualize, clip or save it like any other image. Pixels with NoData in any input band stay NoData.

      Give a trained clusterer, or an untrained one (cluster.kMeans(5)) to train it on this image in the same step. When training this way, numPixels, seed and region control the training sample.

      clusters = img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5))                        # train and apply in one step
clusters = img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5), numPixels=20000, seed=3)
clusters = img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5), region=aoi)            # trained inside aoi

      clusters = img.cluster(trained)
clusters.visualize(labels={0: "Vegetation", 1: "Built-up", 2: "Water", 3: "Forest", 4: "Mixed"},
                   palette=["9ACD32", "D7191C", "1F78B4", "006400", "D2B48C"])
clusters.save("clusters.tif")                    # uint8, NoData = 255
img.clip(aoi).cluster(trained)                   # cluster just an area
clusters.eq(2)                                   # a mask of one cluster

      The image must have the bands the clusterer was trained on (trained.schema()). Extra bands are ignored.

      Vector.cluster(clusterer, outputName="cluster", columns=None, region=None)

      Adds a column with each feature's cluster number. Rows with an empty input get an empty cluster. With an untrained clusterer, it's trained on this dataset's columns (default: all numeric columns), using only the features inside region if given. See Clustering tables.

      Inspecting a trained clusterer

      Member Returns
      trained.nClusters Number of clusters (the chosen number, for cascade and X-means).
      trained.schema() The bands or columns it was trained on.
      trained.centers() The cluster centres in the original units, as a table (one row per cluster).
      trained.info() Prints the method, settings, cluster sizes, centres and scores; returns them as a dict. 

      trained.nClusters                 # 5
trained.schema()                  # ['B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'B8', 'B11', 'B12']
trained.centers()                 # one row per cluster
trained.info()

      ========================================================
 Clusterer   : wekaKMeans
 Settings    : nClusters=5, init='kmeans++', distanceFunction='Euclidean', maxIterations=500, restarts=3, normalize=True
 Inputs      : ['B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'B8', 'B11', 'B12']
 Samples     : 5000
 Clusters    : 5
 Sizes       : [1401, 145, 795, 1635, 1024]
 Centres:
                   B2         B3         B4         B8        B11        B12
   cluster
   0         522.7630   713.1049   745.8926  2215.2709  1947.2819  1378.0546
   1        1512.1621  1836.3966  2200.4310  2866.3069  2991.3448  2749.1690
   2         285.8774   375.4748   260.3239   204.0805   121.3849    79.5459
   ...
========================================================

      Cluster 2 has very low values in every band, including NIR (B8) and SWIR (B11, B12), which is typical of water. Cluster 1 is bright in every band (roads, roofs).

      Choosing the number of clusters

      • You know roughly how many classes you expect: use kMeans or wekaKMeans with that number, or a few more and merge some afterwards with mergeClasses().
      • You don't: let wekaCascadeKMeans or wekaXMeans choose within a range, and look at the scores in info(). Real images often have no single "right" number. When the score keeps improving up to maxClusters, the data supports more detail, so pick the number that is most useful for your map.

      Clustering tables

      Tables and vector datasets are clustered on their numeric columns. Because columns often have different units, use normalize=True.

      from earthforge import vector, cluster

stations = vector.Open("sample_data/stations.csv")
trained = cluster.kMeans(4, normalize=True).train(
    stations, inputProperties=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c"])
grouped = stations.cluster(trained)
grouped.show(5, columns=["station_id", "ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c", "cluster"])
grouped.visualize(column="cluster")

# one step, and trained only on the stations inside a region
stations.cluster(cluster.kMeans(4, normalize=True), columns=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c"])
stations.cluster(cluster.kMeans(3), columns=["ndvi", "temp_c"], region=central)   # all 600 get a cluster

      Memory and speed

      • Training keeps just the sample in memory. The pixels are collected with img.sample(), which reads only the tiles that hold sampled pixels when they are spread thinly over a large image. Training kMeans(4) on 5,000 pixels of a 30,000 × 30,000 raster (2.9 GB) took 7.7 s.
      • Threads: when blocks are processed in parallel, numpy and scikit-learn are limited to one thread per worker, so they don't compete with the workers for the CPU cores.
      • Applying works like every other image operation: block by block, with the model applied to 262,144 pixels at a time. Measured on an 8000 × 8000 × 4-band raster with 6 clusters:
      Time Peak memory
      Train kMeans(6) on 20,000 pixels 1.5 s small
      Cluster and save, 1 worker 11.4 s 60 MB
      Cluster and save, default workers 7.0 s 459 MB

      Tips

      • Choose bands with care. Bands that carry different information (visible, NIR, SWIR) separate land covers better than many similar bands. Adding an index such as NDVI often helps: img.addBands(ndvi.rename("NDVI")).
      • Use normalize=True when inputs have very different ranges, e.g. reflectance bands together with NDVI.
      • Reduce many bands first with PCA: cluster the first few components.
      • Fix the seed to get the same clusters every run.
      PreviousReclassify & classesNextPCA

      User guide

      PCA (principal component analysis)

      PCA turns many correlated bands or columns into a few uncorrelated principal components. PC1 holds the most variation, PC2 the most of what is left, and so on, so the first few components usually summarize the data. Use it to:

      • compress many bands into 2–3 that keep almost all the information,
      • make contrast-rich composites (PC1, PC2, PC3 as RGB),
      • reduce inputs before clustering.
      from earthforge import raster, pca

img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif").select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11", "B12")

model = pca.PCA(3).train(img, numPixels=10000)    # learn the components from a sample
model.info()                                      # explained variance and loadings

pcs = img.pca(model)                              # lazy image: bands PC1, PC2, PC3
pcs.visualize(bands=["PC1", "PC2", "PC3"])
pcs.save("pca.tif")                               # streamed block by block


      ========================================================
 PCA of      : ['B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'B8', 'B11', 'B12']
 Samples     : 10000   standardized: False
   PC1    75.56 %   cumulative  75.56 %
   PC2    19.45 %   cumulative  95.02 %
   PC3     4.23 %   cumulative  99.25 %
 Loadings:
          PC1    PC2    PC3
   B2   0.149 -0.270 -0.402
   B3   0.193 -0.268 -0.441
   B4   0.268 -0.419 -0.406
   B8   0.567  0.734 -0.335
   B11  0.569 -0.065  0.516
   B12  0.473 -0.371  0.318
========================================================

      Three components keep 99.25% of the variation of six bands. PC1 is overall brightness (all loadings positive); PC2 contrasts NIR (B8, positive) with visible and SWIR (negative), much like a vegetation index.

      pca.PCA(nComponents=None, standardize=False)

      Creates a PCA, ready to be trained.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      nComponents int all Number of components to keep. Default: as many as there are inputs.
      standardize bool False Scale every input to unit variance first (correlation PCA). Use it when inputs have different units or ranges, e.g. NDVI, elevation and rainfall. Leave it off for bands of one sensor. 
      pca.PCA(3)
pca.PCA(standardize=True)                     # all components, correlation PCA

      Raises: ValueError if nComponents is not a positive whole number.

      PCA.train(data, inputProperties=None, numPixels=10000, seed=0, region=None)

      Learns the components from an image sample or a dataset's columns.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      data Image or Vector – Image: numPixels random pixels are sampled (block by block). Vector: its numeric columns are used.
      inputProperties list of str all The bands or columns to use.
      numPixels int 10000 Pixels to sample from an image.
      seed int 0 Random seed for the sample.
      region Vector – Learn the components only from pixels (or rows) inside these shapes. The full numPixels are drawn inside the region.

      Returns: a TrainedPCA.

      Raises: ValueError if nComponents is larger than the number of inputs, there are too few valid samples, or the region doesn't overlap the image; TypeError if region isn't a Vector.

      model = pca.PCA(3).train(img)
model = pca.PCA(2).train(img, inputProperties=["B4", "B8", "B11", "B12"], numPixels=20000)

      Training inside a region

      Pass region= to learn the components from your study area only, for example a district, a field or a watershed. The model can then be applied to the region or to the whole image.

      from earthforge import vector

districts = vector.Open("sample_data/districts.geojson")
central = districts.filter(vector.Filter.eq("district", "Central"))

model = pca.PCA(2).train(img, region=central)        # 10,000 pixels, all inside Central
model.explainedVariance()                            # [0.909, 0.080]: one dominant component here
img.clip(central).pca(model).visualize(bands="PC1")  # components of the region only
img.pca(model)                                       # or of the whole image

local = img.pca(2, region=central)                   # train inside the region and apply, in one step

      Sampling with your own geometry

      The region can be any geometry you define yourself. No file is needed (see Creating your own geometries):

      from earthforge import vector

# a rectangle from coordinates (longitude, latitude)
box = vector.Rectangle(73.11, 33.69, 73.14, 33.71)
model = pca.PCA(3).train(img, region=box)

# a polygon from its corners
lake = vector.Polygon([(73.110, 33.690), (73.145, 33.692), (73.148, 33.716), (73.118, 33.712)])
model = pca.PCA(3).train(img, region=lake)
model.explainedVariance()                       # [0.887, 0.097, 0.013]

# a circle of 500 m around a point
circle = vector.Point(73.125, 33.700).buffer(500)
pcs = img.pca(3, region=circle)                 # train inside the circle and apply, in one step

# a shape drawn on geojson.io (paste the GeoJSON), or WKT text
drawn = vector.fromGeometry({"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[73.11, 33.69], [73.14, 33.69],
                                                                 [73.14, 33.71], [73.11, 33.69]]]})
model = pca.PCA(2).train(img, region=drawn)

# coordinates in another CRS (UTM metres): reprojected automatically
box_utm = vector.Rectangle(323500, 3729500, 326500, 3731500, crs="EPSG:32643")
model = pca.PCA(2).train(img, region=box_utm)

# several areas at once
from shapely.geometry import box as shape_box
areas = vector.fromGeometry([shape_box(73.10, 33.70, 73.11, 33.71), shape_box(73.15, 33.68, 73.16, 33.69)])
model = pca.PCA(3).train(img, region=areas)     # pixels from both areas

      You can also sample first and keep the sample, for example to inspect or save it, then train on it:

      samples = img.sample(10000, region=lake)        # 10,000 pixels, all inside the polygon
samples.show(5)
samples.save("lake_pixels.csv")
model = pca.PCA(3).train(samples)

      All numPixels are drawn inside the geometry, as long as it covers that many pixels.

      The components describe the variation inside the region, so they differ from components learned on the whole image. For the six bands above, PC1 explains 76% of the variation of the whole scene but 91% within the Central district, which is mostly lake and shore.

      The results match scikit-learn's PCA on the same sample.

      The trained model

      Member Returns
      model.nComponents Number of components.
      model.schema() The bands or columns it was trained on.
      model.componentNames() Output names: ['PC1', 'PC2', ...].
      model.explainedVariance() Share of the total variance each component explains (0–1).
      model.loadings() Table of how much each input contributes to each component.
      model.info() Prints explained variance and loadings; returns a dict. 
      model.nComponents                  # 3
model.schema()                     # ['B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'B8', 'B11', 'B12']
model.componentNames()             # ['PC1', 'PC2', 'PC3']
model.explainedVariance()          # [0.7556, 0.1945, 0.0423]
sum(model.explainedVariance())     # 0.9925: share kept by the 3 components
model.loadings()                   # inputs x components
model.info()

      Applying: img.pca() and vector.pca()

      Image.pca(model, numPixels=10000, standardize=False, seed=0, region=None)

      Transforms the image into its principal components: a lazy image with float32 bands PC1, PC2, ... Give a trained model, or a number of components to train one on this image right away. When training this way, region= limits the training pixels to a geometry; the whole image is still transformed.

      pcs = img.pca(model)                        # with a trained model
quick = img.pca(3)                          # train and apply in one step
all_pcs = img.pca(None, standardize=True)   # all components, correlation PCA

pcs.select("PC1").visualize(palette="gray")
pcs.select("PC1", "PC2").save("pc12.tif")

      The image must have the bands the model was trained on. Pixels with NoData in any input stay NoData. You can apply a model trained on one image to another image with the same bands, e.g. another date.

      Vector.pca(model, columns=None, standardize=False)

      Adds columns PC1, PC2, ... to a table or vector dataset.

      from earthforge import vector

stations = vector.Open("sample_data/stations.csv")
with_pcs = stations.pca(2, columns=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "rain_mm", "temp_c"], standardize=True)
with_pcs.show(5, columns=["station_id", "PC1", "PC2"])

# or with a model you keep
model = pca.PCA(2, standardize=True).train(stations, inputProperties=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c"])
stations.pca(model)

      Rows with an empty value in any input column get empty components.

      PCA, then clustering

      Cluster on the first few components instead of many raw bands:

      from earthforge import cluster

pcs = img.pca(pca.PCA(3).train(img))
trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(pcs, numPixels=5000)
pcs.cluster(trained).visualize(labels={i: f"Cluster {i}" for i in range(5)})

      Memory and speed

      Training reads only a sample, and on large images only the tiles that hold sampled pixels: training on 10,000 pixels of a 30,000 × 30,000 raster (2.9 GB) took 2.8 s. Applying works block by block. On an 8000 × 8000 × 4-band raster, saving 3 components took 22 s with 1 worker (peak 79 MB) and 15 s with the default workers (peak 575 MB). All components of a block are computed together, so the inputs are read once.

      PreviousClusteringNextMosaic

      User guide

      Mosaic

      raster.mosaic() combines many rasters (tiles, scenes, or computed images) into one image without loading them into memory. It works like a GDAL virtual raster (VRT): creating the mosaic reads only each file's metadata, and pixels are read later, only where and when they are needed.

      from earthforge import raster

m = raster.mosaic("tiles/")                    # every .tif in a folder
m.meta()
m.select("B4", "B3", "B2").visualize(min=0, max=3000)
m.save("mosaic.tif")                           # streamed, with a progress bar

      Saving mosaic.tif: 100%|██████████| 256/256 [00:08<00:00, 30.5block/s]
Saved: C:\...\mosaic.tif  (4 band(s), uint16)

      How memory stays low

      Step What is read
      raster.mosaic(...) Only the metadata of each file (size, position, CRS, bands).
      visualize() A downsampled preview, with the longest side ≤ max_size pixels.
      save() The mosaic is written in 1024 × 1024 pixel blocks, one band at a time. For each block, only the part of each tile that overlaps the block is read.
      clip(aoi) Only the tiles and pixels inside the area of interest.

      Memory use depends on the block size (about 4 MB per band per block), not on the size of the inputs. Measured on a mosaic of 9 overlapping tiles totalling 8000 × 8000 px × 4 bands (512 MB): saving peaked at 22 MB of memory and took 8.5 s, and the result was identical to the original raster.

      A mosaic is an ordinary lazy Image, so you can chain anything on it before saving: select, band math, normalizedDifference, clip, where, … Each step still reads only what it needs.

      Signature

      raster.mosaic(images, method="last", res=None, save=False)
      Parameter Type Default Description
      images list, folder, or pattern – A list of Images and/or file paths; a folder (all .tif/.tiff files); or a glob pattern such as "tiles/*.tif" or "scenes/**/B04.tif".
      method str "last" How overlapping pixels are combined. See Methods.
      res number or (x, y) first image's Pixel size of the mosaic. Images with a different pixel size are resampled (nearest neighbour).
      save bool or str False True saves mosaic_mosaic_<epoch>.tif; a string saves to that path.

      Returns: Image covering the union of all inputs. Band names come from the first image.

      Raises: ValueError if no rasters are found, the CRSs or band counts differ, or method/res are invalid.

      Methods

      method Overlapping pixels get…
      "last" the value of the last image in the list (later images on top)
      "first" the value of the first image in the list (earlier images on top)
      "min" the smallest value
      "max" the largest value, e.g. a maximum-NDVI composite
      "mean" the average of all images that have data there

      NoData pixels never cover valid ones, whatever the method. A tile's NoData border doesn't hide the tile underneath.

      Rules for the inputs

      • Same CRS. All images must use the same coordinate reference system. Reprojection is not supported yet.
      • Same number of bands. Use .select() first if needed.
      • Any position and pixel size. Tiles may overlap, have gaps (gaps become NoData), sit on different pixel grids, or have different resolutions. Pixels are resampled into the mosaic's grid with nearest neighbour.
      • Computed inputs work. For example, mosaic the NDVI of several scenes:
      paths = ["scene_1.tif", "scene_2.tif", "scene_3.tif"]
ndvis = [raster.image(p).normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]) for p in paths]
raster.mosaic(ndvis, method="max", save="max_ndvi.tif")

      Data type of the saved file

      save() keeps the source's integer type (for example uint16 for Sentinel-2 or Landsat digital numbers) when pixel values pass through unchanged, which is the case for "last", "first", "min" and "max" mosaics of plain files. This keeps the output the same size as the input instead of doubling it to float32. "mean" mosaics and anything computed (band math, indices) are saved as float32.

      NoData pixels in an integer file get the source's NoData value, or 0 if the source has none. If 0 is a real value in your data, choose another one:

      m.save("mosaic.tif", nodata=65535)
m.save("mosaic_f32.tif", dtype="float32")       # force a type

      Large mosaics: tips

      • Many cores help. Mosaic blocks are computed in parallel: about 2× faster with 4–8 workers in our tests. See Many cores and lots of RAM.
      • Clip early. raster.mosaic("tiles/").clip(aoi).save(...) reads only the tiles and pixels inside the area of interest.
      • Pick the compression to suit the job. compress=None writes fastest; "zstd" is fast with good compression; "deflate" (the default) is the most widely supported.
      • Add overviews to big source tiles (gdaladdo) so that visualize() previews are fast. Without them, a preview of a huge mosaic has to touch every block of every tile.
      • Keep the output on a local disk. Writing to a network drive or USB stick is often the slowest part.
      • Many tiles are fine. At most 64 files are kept open at a time, so mosaics of thousands of tiles don't run out of file handles.
      PreviousPCANextVector

      User guide

      vector: vector files and tables

      from earthforge import vector

      Opens vector files (boundaries, points, lines) and tables, shows and filters their records, adds columns, joins datasets, and exports them. Vectors are used to clip images, and an image's extent is itself a vector (img.geometry()).

      aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
aoi.meta()
aoi.columns()                    # ['name', 'area_class']

clipped = img.clip(aoi)
img.geometry().save("extent.geojson")
