      Sample data

      The folder sample_data/ contains example datasets that cover the sample image, used in the examples on this page. Recreate them with python sample_data/make_sample_data.py. The data is random but always the same.

      File Contents
      stations.csv 600 weather stations: station_id, name, district, land_cover, ndvi, longitude, latitude, elevation_m, rain_mm (about 3% empty), temp_c, install_date, active. The NDVI and land cover come from the sample image at each station.
      survey.xlsx Sheets 2023 (220 plots) and 2024 (240 plots) with lon/lat columns; districts, a table without coordinates (district, population, households, area_km2); and notes.
      districts.geojson 5 district polygons (district, code, zone_type) covering the image. 
      from earthforge import vector
from earthforge.vector import Filter

stations = vector.Open("sample_data/stations.csv")                      # 600 points
districts = vector.Open("sample_data/districts.geojson")                # 5 polygons
population = vector.Open("sample_data/survey.xlsx", layer="districts")  # a table

      Supported formats

      Format Extensions Read Write Notes
      Shapefile .shp ✓ ✓ Keep .dbf, .shx, .prj next to it.
      GeoJSON .geojson, .json ✓ ✓ Written in EPSG:4326.
      KML .kml ✓ ✓ All folders are combined; written in EPSG:4326.
      KMZ .kmz ✓ – Zipped KML (Google Earth).
      GeoPackage .gpkg ✓ ✓ Multi-layer: choose with layer=.
      Parquet / GeoParquet .parquet ✓ ✓ Plain Parquet tables are read like CSV.
      CSV .csv ✓ ✓ Points from coordinate columns, shapes from a WKT column, or a plain table.
      Excel .xlsx, .xls ✓ ✓ (.xlsx) Any sheet: choose with layer=.

      vector.Open(path, layer=None, x=None, y=None, crs=None)

      Opens a vector file or table as a Vector. The whole dataset is loaded into memory, which is fine for boundaries, points and tables.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      path str or Path – The file to open.
      layer str or int first Layer of a multi-layer file (GeoPackage, KML folders) or sheet of an Excel file, by name or 0-based index. For KML/KMZ, all layers are combined unless you pick one, and a layer column records where each feature came from.
      x, y str detected Column names with point coordinates in a table. See Tables.
      crs str or int – CRS of the data when the file doesn't define one, e.g. "EPSG:32643".

      Returns: Vector

      Raises: - VectorNotFoundError if the file doesn't exist. - VectorReadError if the format is unsupported or the file can't be read. - ValueError if layer or x/y name something that doesn't exist.

      aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
sites = vector.Open("sites.kmz")
roads = vector.Open("city.gpkg", layer="roads")
survey = vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer="2024")         # sheet by name
survey = vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer=1)              # sheet by index
wells = vector.Open("wells.csv", x="easting", y="northing", crs="EPSG:32643")

      vector.layers(path)

      Lists the layers of a file, or the sheets of an Excel file.

      vector.layers("survey.xlsx")       # ['2023', '2024', 'notes']
vector.layers("city.gpkg")         # ['roads', 'buildings']

      CSV and Parquet files have no layers, so they return [].

      Creating your own geometries

      You don't need a file to make a geometry. These functions create a Vector from coordinates, GeoJSON or WKT. Use it anywhere a vector is accepted: clip(), sample(region=), PCA and clustering training, filterBounds(), overlay=.

      Function Creates
      vector.Rectangle(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax, crs="EPSG:4326") A rectangle from its west, south, east and north edges.
      vector.Polygon([(x, y), ...], crs="EPSG:4326") A polygon from 3 or more corners (closed automatically).
      vector.Point(x, y, crs="EPSG:4326") A point; add .buffer(metres) for a circle.
      vector.fromGeometry(geometry, crs="EPSG:4326", properties=None) Anything else: GeoJSON (a geometry, Feature or FeatureCollection), WKT text, shapely shapes, or a list of several.
      vector.buffer(distance) (a method) Grows each geometry by distance metres (negative shrinks). Works in metres for longitude/latitude data too.

      The default CRS "EPSG:4326" means longitude, latitude in degrees, in that order (x = longitude). For projected coordinates pass the CRS, e.g. crs="EPSG:32643" for UTM zone 43N.

      from earthforge import vector

box = vector.Rectangle(73.11, 33.69, 73.14, 33.71)                    # lon/lat
box_utm = vector.Rectangle(323500, 3729500, 326500, 3731500, crs="EPSG:32643")

lake = vector.Polygon([(73.110, 33.690), (73.145, 33.692), (73.148, 33.716), (73.118, 33.712)])

site = vector.Point(73.125, 33.700)
circle = site.buffer(500)                                              # 500 m around the point

# GeoJSON, e.g. copied from geojson.io (a geometry, a Feature or a FeatureCollection)
drawn = vector.fromGeometry({
    "type": "Polygon",
    "coordinates": [[[73.11, 33.69], [73.14, 33.69], [73.14, 33.71], [73.11, 33.71], [73.11, 33.69]]],
})

# WKT text
wkt = vector.fromGeometry("POLYGON ((73.11 33.69, 73.14 33.69, 73.14 33.71, 73.11 33.69))")

# several training areas with names
from shapely.geometry import box as shape_box
fields = vector.fromGeometry([shape_box(73.10, 33.70, 73.11, 33.71), shape_box(73.15, 33.68, 73.16, 33.69)],
                             properties={"name": ["north field", "south field"]})

corridor = vector.Open("roads.geojson").buffer(50)                     # 50 m each side of the roads
inner = vector.Open("boundary.shp").buffer(-100)                       # 100 m inside the boundary

      The results are ordinary vectors: fields.show(), fields.visualize(), fields.save("fields.geojson") all work.

      Raises: ValueError for a rectangle with xmin >= xmax or ymin >= ymax, a polygon with fewer than 3 corners or crossing edges, unreadable WKT, or properties with the wrong length; TypeError for anything that isn't a geometry.

      Vector attributes

      Attribute Type Description
      path str The file it was opened from.
      data GeoDataFrame The features, as a geopandas GeoDataFrame. For a table without geometry, this is a pandas DataFrame.
      crs pyproj.CRS or None Coordinate reference system. None if unknown or for a plain table.
      bounds tuple or None (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in the vector's CRS. 
      aoi.path                                     # 'boundary.shp'
aoi.crs.to_epsg()                            # 4326
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = aoi.bounds
lake = aoi.data[aoi.data["name"] == "lake"]  # any geopandas operation

      print(aoi) shows a one-line summary and the first 5 rows:

      <Vector stations.csv | 3 features | Point | EPSG:4326>
  station  Latitude  Longitude  rain_mm             geometry
0       A     33.70      73.10     12.5    POINT (73.1 33.7)
1       B     33.71      73.12      8.0  POINT (73.12 33.71)
2       C     33.72      73.15     15.2  POINT (73.15 33.72)

      Vector.meta()

      Prints a summary and returns it as a dict with path, format, layer, layers, features, geometryTypes, crs, bounds and columns (name → data type).

      vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer="2024").meta()

      ==================================================
 Metadata for: survey.xlsx
==================================================
 Format     : Excel
 Layer      : 2024   (available: ['2023', '2024', 'notes'])
 Features   : 3
 Geometry   : Point (3)
 CRS        : EPSG:4326
 Bounds     : (73.100000, 33.700000, 73.150000, 33.720000)
 Columns    : 4
   station    str
   Latitude   float64
   Longitude  float64
   rain_mm    int64
==================================================

      Vector.columnNames()

      Returns the attribute column names, like bandNames() does for images. The geometry column is not included. The result is a ColumnList: a normal list with .size() and .get(i). columns() does the same.

      stations.columnNames()               # ['station_id', 'name', 'district', 'land_cover', 'ndvi', ...]
stations.columnNames().size()        # 12
stations.columnNames().get(0)        # 'station_id'
"rain_mm" in stations.columnNames()  # True
aoi.columns()                        # same as aoi.columnNames()

      Vector.size(), hasGeometry(), geometryTypes()

      Method Returns
      size() Number of features (rows). len(aoi) also works.
      hasGeometry() True for features with geometries, False for a plain table.
      geometryTypes() Geometry types and their counts, e.g. {"Polygon": 12, "MultiPolygon": 2}. 
      aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
aoi.size()                                   # 2  (same as len(aoi))
aoi.hasGeometry()                            # True
aoi.geometryTypes()                          # {'Polygon': 2}

vector.Open("population.csv").hasGeometry()  # False: a table without coordinates
vector.Open("stations.csv").geometryTypes()  # {'Point': 3}

      Showing records: show()

      Vector.show(n=10, columns=None)

      Shows records as a table: the first n, or all of them with "all". In Jupyter it's displayed as a formatted table; elsewhere it's printed. Geometries appear as short WKT text.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      n int or "all" 10 How many records to show from the top. "all" (or None) shows every record.
      columns list of str all Only show these columns. 

      stations.show()                                          # first 10
stations.show(25)                                        # first 25
stations.show("all")                                     # all 600
stations.show(3, columns=["station_id", "district", "rain_mm"])

      stations.csv: showing 3 of 600 records
  station_id district  rain_mm
0     ST0001     East      5.8
1     ST0002    North      4.9
2     ST0003    North      6.5

      Combine it with the other methods: stations.filter(...).show(), stations.sort("rain_mm").show(5).

      Getting values: get(), first()

      Vector.get(key) returns either a column's values or one feature:

      Call Returns
      stations.get("rain_mm") All values of the column, as a list.
      stations.get(0) The feature at that position, as a Feature. Negative numbers count from the end (-1 is the last).
      stations.first() The first feature, the same as get(0). 
      rain = stations.get("rain_mm")             # list of 600 values
len(rain), max(r for r in rain if r == r)  # skip the empty (NaN) readings

f = stations.get(0)
f.get("district")                          # 'East'
f.properties()                             # all properties as a dict
stations.get(-1).get("station_id")         # 'ST0600'

      Raises: ValueError if the column doesn't exist or the position is out of range; TypeError for anything other than a name or a number.

      Filtering: filter() and Filter

      Vector.filter(filter) keeps the features that pass a condition. Build conditions with Filter and combine them with & (and), | (or) and ~ (not):

      from earthforge.vector import Filter

north = stations.filter(Filter.eq("district", "North"))
wet = stations.filter(Filter.gt("rain_mm", 20))
north_forest = stations.filter(Filter.eq("district", "North") & Filter.eq("land_cover", "forest"))
not_north = stations.filter(~Filter.eq("district", "North"))
water_or_negative = stations.filter(Filter.Or(Filter.eq("land_cover", "water"), Filter.lt("ndvi", 0)))
north.size()                               # 129
      Filter Keeps features where…
      Filter.eq(name, value) the property equals value
      Filter.neq(name, value) the property is not value
      Filter.lt(name, value) / Filter.lte(name, value) the property is less than (or equal to) value
      Filter.gt(name, value) / Filter.gte(name, value) the property is greater than (or equal to) value
      Filter.rangeContains(name, min, max) min <= property <= max
      Filter.inList(name, values) the property is one of values
      Filter.stringContains(name, text, ignoreCase=False) the text contains text
      Filter.stringStartsWith(name, text) / Filter.stringEndsWith(name, text) the text starts / ends with text
      Filter.notNull(name, ...) all the given properties have a value
      Filter.isNull(name) the property is empty (NaN)
      Filter.And(f1, f2, ...) or f1 & f2 all filters pass
      Filter.Or(f1, f2, ...) or f1 \| f2 any filter passes
      Filter.Not(f) or ~f the filter doesn't pass 
      stations.filter(Filter.rangeContains("ndvi", 0.2, 0.5))
stations.filter(Filter.inList("district", ["North", "East"]))
stations.filter(Filter.stringContains("name", "lake", ignoreCase=True))
stations.filter(Filter.stringStartsWith("station_id", "ST00"))
stations.filter(Filter.stringEndsWith("name", "0"))     # names ending in 0
stations.filter(Filter.notNull("rain_mm", "temp_c"))
stations.filter(Filter.isNull("rain_mm"))              # 20 stations without a reading

      Empty values (NaN) never pass a comparison, so Filter.gt("rain_mm", 20) skips stations without a reading.

      By location: filterBounds()

      Vector.filterBounds(geometry) keeps the features that intersect a vector or an image's extent. The geometry is reprojected automatically.

      central = districts.filter(Filter.eq("district", "Central"))
stations.filterBounds(central).size()      # 105 stations inside the Central district
stations.filterBounds(img)                 # stations inside the image

      Sorting: sort(), limit()

      Method Returns
      sort(column, ascending=True) All features, sorted by column.
      limit(n, column=None, ascending=True) The first n features, sorted by column first if given. 
      stations.sort("elevation_m").show(5)                      # 5 lowest
stations.limit(10, "rain_mm", ascending=False).show()     # 10 wettest
stations.limit(100)                                       # first 100

      Adding columns: map() and Feature

      Vector.map(func) runs a function on every feature and builds a new dataset from what it returns. The function receives a Feature and returns a Feature:

      • f.set({...}) keeps the geometry and adds or changes properties. This is how you add columns.
      • vector.Feature(geometry, {...}) builds a feature with a new geometry and properties.
      • None drops the feature.
      def add_columns(f):
    rain = f.get("rain_mm")
    return f.set({
        "rain_cm": rain / 10,
        "wet": rain > 20,
        "label": f.get("district") + " / " + f.get("land_cover"),
    })

stations2 = stations.map(add_columns)
stations2.show(3, columns=["station_id", "rain_mm", "rain_cm", "wet", "label"])

# area and perimeter of each district
districts.map(lambda f: f.set({"area_km2": f.area() / 1e6, "perimeter_km": f.length() / 1000}))

# new geometry: district centre points
centres = districts.map(lambda f: vector.Feature(f.centroid(), {"district": f.get("district")}))

# keep only active stations
active = stations.map(lambda f: f if f.get("active") else None)

      Empty values come through as NaN. NaN > 20 is False, and NaN / 10 is NaN.

      Feature

      A feature is one geometry plus its properties. Features don't change in place: set() returns a new one.

      Method Returns
      vector.Feature(geometry, properties) A new feature. geometry is a shapely geometry, a GeoJSON dict, or None.
      f.get(name) The value of one property.
      f.set({...}) / f.set(name, value) A copy with properties added or changed.
      f.properties() All properties as a dict.
      f.propertyNames() The property names.
      f.geometry() The shapely geometry.
      f.area() Area in m², measured on the WGS84 ellipsoid for longitude/latitude data.
      f.length() Length of a line, or perimeter of a polygon, in metres.
      f.centroid() The centre point. 
      from shapely.geometry import Point

f = vector.Feature(Point(73.12, 33.70), {"name": "New station"})
f = f.set("rain_mm", 12.5)
f.get("rain_mm")                    # 12.5
f.propertyNames()                   # ['name', 'rain_mm']
f.geometry()                        # POINT (73.12 33.7)
districts.first().area() / 1e6      # about 6.75 km²
districts.first().centroid()        # POINT (73.1266 33.7048)

      Combining datasets: merge(), join(), spatialJoin()

      Method What it does
      merge(other) Appends the features of other (stacks the rows).
      join(other, on, right_on=None, how="inner") Adds the columns of other to each feature by matching values in a column. other can be a table.
      spatialJoin(other, predicate="intersects", how="inner") Adds the columns of the features of other that each feature touches (or lies "within", "contains", ...). 
      # merge: both survey years in one dataset
plots = vector.Open("sample_data/survey.xlsx", layer="2023").merge(
        vector.Open("sample_data/survey.xlsx", layer="2024"))
plots.size()                                              # 460

# join by attribute: add population figures to each station
population = vector.Open("sample_data/survey.xlsx", layer="districts")
stations.join(population, on="district").show(3, columns=["station_id", "district", "population"])
districts.join(population, on="district", how="left")      # polygons + population

# join by location: which district polygon is each station in?
with_zone = stations.spatialJoin(districts, predicate="within")
with_zone.show(3, columns=["station_id", "code", "zone_type"])
      • how: "inner" keeps only features with a match; "left" keeps all features, and unmatched ones get empty values.
      • Clashing names: columns that exist in both datasets get the suffix _2 from other (e.g. district_2).
      • Several matches: in a spatial join, a feature that matches several features of other appears once per match.
      • Reprojection: other is reprojected to this dataset's CRS automatically.

      Clustering and PCA of columns

      Vector.cluster(clusterer, outputName="cluster", columns=None, region=None) adds each row's cluster number. Give a trained clusterer, or an untrained one to train it on columns (only on the rows inside region if given). Vector.pca(model, columns=None, standardize=False) adds principal-component columns PC1, PC2, ... Rows with an empty input value get empty results. See Clustering and PCA.

      from earthforge import cluster

trained = cluster.kMeans(4, normalize=True).train(stations, inputProperties=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c"])
grouped = stations.cluster(trained)
grouped.show(5, columns=["station_id", "ndvi", "elevation_m", "cluster"])
stations.cluster(cluster.kMeans(3), columns=["ndvi", "temp_c"], region=central)   # train in one step

with_pcs = stations.pca(2, columns=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "rain_mm", "temp_c"], standardize=True)
with_pcs.show(5, columns=["station_id", "PC1", "PC2"])

      Vector.visualize()

      Vector.visualize(column=None, palette=None, color=None, edgecolor=None, linewidth=1.0,
                 legend=True, save_chart=False, dpi=200)

      Draws the geometries as a map chart. Polygons are drawn filled with an outline, lines as lines and points as dots. The axes show map coordinates (longitude/latitude for geographic CRSs).

      Parameter Type Default Description
      column str – Attribute column to color the features by. Numbers get a palette and a colorbar; text gets one color per value and a legend.
      palette str or list "viridis" (numbers), "tab10" (text) Palette for column: any built-in palette, matplotlib colormap or list of colors.
      color str green Fill color when no column is given. "none" draws outlines only.
      edgecolor str dark green Outline color. When coloring by column, the default is white for polygons and dark grey for points.
      linewidth float 1.0 Outline or line width.
      legend bool True Show the colorbar or legend when column is given.
      save_chart bool False Also save the chart as <file name>_<epoch>.png in the current folder.
      dpi int 200 Resolution of the saved PNG.

      Returns: the saved file name when save_chart=True, otherwise None.

      Raises: ValueError if the dataset is a table without geometries, or column doesn't exist.

      aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
aoi.visualize()                                          # filled shapes with outlines
aoi.visualize(color="none", edgecolor="red")             # outlines only
aoi.visualize(column="name")                             # one color per name, with a legend

stations = vector.Open("stations.csv")
stations.visualize(column="rain_mm", palette="precipitation", save_chart=True)
      aoi.visualize(column="name") stations.visualize(column="rain_mm", palette="precipitation")

      For more control (labels, basemaps, custom styling), use geopandas directly: aoi.data.plot(...).

      Drawing vectors on an image

      Pass vectors to Image.visualize() with overlay= to draw them on top of the image. Polygons are drawn as outlines, lines as lines and points as dots. Vectors in another CRS are reprojected to the image's CRS, and the map keeps the image's extent.

      img.visualize(bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], overlay=aoi)                       # red outlines
img.visualize(bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], overlay=aoi, overlay_color="yellow")

# several vectors, one color each
img.visualize(bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], gamma=1.2,
              overlay=[aoi, roads, stations], overlay_color=["red", "yellow", "cyan"])

# on an index too
img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).visualize(min=-0.2, max=0.8, palette="ndvi", overlay=aoi)

      Vector.toGeoJSON()

      Returns the features as a GeoJSON dict, with coordinates in EPSG:4326 (longitude, latitude).

      gj = img.geometry().toGeoJSON()
gj["features"][0]["geometry"]["coordinates"]
# [[[73.09232, 33.72958], [73.16086, 33.72958], [73.16086, 33.68009], [73.09232, 33.68009], [73.09232, 33.72958]]]

      Vector.save(path)

      Writes the dataset to a file. The format is chosen from the extension: .geojson/.json, .shp, .gpkg, .kml, .parquet, .csv or .xlsx.

      • GeoJSON and KML are always written in EPSG:4326, as those formats require. Other formats keep the vector's CRS.
      • In .csv and .xlsx, geometries are written as WKT text in a geometry column. Opening that file again turns them back into shapes.
      • Tables without geometry can only be saved as .csv, .xlsx or .parquet.

      Returns: the absolute path of the saved file.

      img.geometry().save("extent.geojson")
aoi.save("aoi.gpkg")
vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer="2024").save("survey_2024.geojson")    # table → GeoJSON points

      Tables: CSV, Excel, Parquet

      Tables are turned into features automatically:

      1. Coordinate columns → points. Recognised names (case-insensitive) are longitude/lon/long/lng/x and latitude/lat/y. Name them yourself with x= and y=. When all values are within ±180 / ±90, the CRS is assumed to be EPSG:4326; otherwise pass crs=.
      2. WKT column → shapes. A column named wkt, geometry, geom, the_geom or shape that contains WKT text such as POLYGON ((…)). Pass crs=, because WKT doesn't record a CRS.
      3. Otherwise → a plain table. meta(), columns(), size(), data and save() (as .csv, .xlsx or .parquet) still work, but it can't be used to clip.

      GeoParquet files (Parquet with geometry metadata, for example written by geopandas) are read directly with their CRS.

      PreviousMosaicNextPalettes & legends

      User guide

      Palettes

      The palette argument of visualize() colors single-band images and draws a matching colorbar.

      img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).visualize(min=-0.2, max=0.8, palette="ndvi")

      Ways to specify a palette

      Form Example Notes
      Built-in name "ndvi", "temperature" See the table below.
      matplotlib colormap "viridis", "RdYlGn", "terrain" All matplotlib colormaps.
      Reversed "ndvi_r", "RdYlGn_r" Add _r to any name.
      List of colors ["0000FF", "FFFFFF", "008000"] 2 or more colors, evenly spaced from min to max. Hex with or without #, or names like "blue".

      If a built-in name and a matplotlib name are the same, the built-in palette is used.

      Built-in palettes

      Name Good for Low → high
      ndvi NDVI white/bare → brown → green → dark green
      evi EVI, vegetation vigor brown → beige → green
      vegetation Any vegetation index red → yellow → green
      ndwi NDWI / water indices brown (dry) → beige → blue (water)
      water Water depth, MNDWI, turbidity white → dark blue
      precipitation Rainfall white → cyan → blue → purple → orange → red
      soil_moisture Soil moisture brown (dry) → teal (wet)
      ndbi Built-up index blue → yellow → red (urban)
      nbr Burn ratio red (burned) → yellow → green (healthy)
      ndsi Snow index black → gray → white (snow)
      elevation DEMs green (low) → light green → brown → gray → white (peaks)
      temperature Land surface temperature dark blue → cyan → green → yellow → red (MODIS LST palette)
      night_lights Night-time lights (VIIRS) black → purple → orange → white
      diverging Anomalies centered on 0 red → white → blue
      change Change detection (loss/gain) red (loss) → white → green (gain)
      blue_red General purpose ("rainbow") blue → cyan → green → yellow → red

      Functions

      raster.palettes()

      Returns the built-in palette names as a sorted list.

      raster.palettes()
# ['blue_red', 'change', 'diverging', 'elevation', 'evi', 'nbr', 'ndbi', 'ndsi', 'ndvi', 'ndwi',
#  'night_lights', 'precipitation', 'soil_moisture', 'temperature', 'vegetation', 'water']

      raster.showPalettes(names=None, save_chart=False, dpi=200)

      Shows a color strip for each palette, like the image above.

      Parameter Type Default Description
      names list of str all built-ins + 15 popular matplotlib colormaps Palettes to show.
      save_chart bool False Also saves palettes_<epoch>.png.
      dpi int 200 Resolution of the saved PNG. 
      raster.showPalettes()
raster.showPalettes(["ndvi", "ndvi_r", "viridis", ["red", "yellow", "green"]])

      raster.PALETTES

      The dict that holds the built-in palettes (name → list of hex colors). To add your own palette for the session:

      raster.PALETTES["my_palette"] = ["000000", "FF0000", "FFFF00"]
img.select("B8").visualize(palette="my_palette")

      Legends for class maps

      For categorical images, such as the output of where(), pass labels to get one flat color per class and a legend:

      classes.visualize(labels={1: "Water", 2: "Sparse", 3: "Moderate", 4: "Dense"},
                  palette=["0000FF", "D2B48C", "9ACD32", "006400"])
classes.visualize(labels={1: "Water", 2: "Land"})                 # colors from "tab10"
classes.visualize(labels={1: "Low", 2: "Mid", 3: "High"}, palette="YlGn")   # sampled evenly

      With labels, palette can be a list with one color per class, or a palette name. Qualitative matplotlib maps (tab10, Set1, Paired, …) are used color by color. Other palettes are sampled evenly from end to end. See Showing class maps.

      Colorbar options

      visualize() argument Default Description
      colorbar True Show or hide the colorbar.
      colorbar_label band name Colorbar title.
      colorbar_orientation "vertical" "vertical" puts it to the right of the map, "horizontal" below it.

      The colorbar shows real pixel values from min to max. The arrows at each end mean values outside that range are clipped to the end colors.

      PreviousVectorNextMemory & performance

      User guide

      Memory and performance

      The library is designed so memory use depends on what you look at or save, not on the size of the raster.

      How it works

      1. Lazy images. raster.image() and raster.mosaic() read only metadata. select(), rename(), addBands(), band math, normalizedDifference(), clip() and the rest build a small recipe (a tree of operations) and read no pixels.
      2. Previews for display. visualize() asks GDAL for a downsampled read (out_shape), at most max_size pixels (default 1500) on the longest side. GDAL uses the file's overviews if it has any.
      3. Streaming for export. save() computes and writes the image in 1024 × 1024 pixel blocks (aligned to the 256-px output tiles), one band at a time: about 4 MB per band per step. Square blocks keep this small even for very wide images. A full-width strip of a 200,000-px-wide mosaic would need about 200 MB per band.
      4. float32 for computing, integer types kept on disk. Pixels are read as float32, half the memory of float64. When values pass through unchanged, save() writes the source's integer type (e.g. uint16), so the output isn't twice the size of the input.
      5. Reads are shared within a band. In normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]), B8 and B4 are each read once, although the formula uses each of them twice. The cache is cleared after every output band.
      6. Figures are closed after they are shown, so matplotlib doesn't keep them in memory.
      7. Clipping crops. clip() reads only the window covering the vector's bounding box, so a small area of interest in a huge raster reads only that area. The polygon mask is rasterized window by window.
      8. Mosaics read only overlaps. For each block, a mosaic reads only the part of each tile that overlaps the block. Tiles that don't overlap are skipped with a quick bounds check.
      9. Open files are capped. At most 64 source files are open at once per worker (least recently used are closed), so mosaics of thousands of tiles work.
      10. Blocks are computed in parallel on computers with several cores, within a memory budget. See Many cores and lots of RAM.
      11. Sampling reads only what it needs. img.sample(), which clustering and PCA use for training, reads only the small tiles that hold sampled pixels when samples are spread thinly over a large image, and whole blocks when they are dense. On a 200,000 × 200,000 mosaic, 5,000 samples read about 5,000 small tiles instead of all 38,000+ blocks.
      12. Applying models is chunked. Clusterers and PCA are applied to 262,144 pixels at a time, and the memory budget counts their inputs. When blocks run in parallel, numpy and scikit-learn are limited to one thread per worker.
      13. Vectors load on demand. from earthforge import raster doesn't import geopandas. It is loaded the first time you use vector, clip(), geometry() or bounds(save=...).

      Many cores and lots of RAM

      save() adapts to the computer it runs on:

      • Workers. Blocks are computed in parallel threads, one per CPU core, up to 8 by default. Each worker has its own open files. One block, with all its bands, is one task, so each source tile is decompressed only once.
      • Memory budget. The number of blocks in progress is capped at about a quarter of the free RAM (between 256 MB and 8 GB). A PC with little free memory automatically uses fewer workers, and a PC with lots of RAM keeps more blocks in progress.
      • Compression always uses every core: GDAL compresses blocks in parallel while they're written.
      Computer What happens
      2–4 cores, 4–8 GB RAM 2–4 workers; memory for blocks typically 50–200 MB.
      8+ cores, 16+ GB RAM 8 workers, 16 blocks in progress; a few hundred MB. Raise raster.MAX_WORKERS to use more cores.
      Limited by the disk Extra cores help little: writing (and compressing) the output is the slowest part.

      Measured on a 20-core PC, 8000 × 8000 raster (best of 3 runs). The outputs are identical whatever the number of workers:

      Job Compression 1 worker 4 workers 8 workers
      NDVI, 1 band none 3.0 s 1.4 s 1.9 s
      NDVI, 1 band deflate 7.4 s 5.4 s 5.5 s
      × 0.0001, 4 bands none 10.5 s 10.8 s 10.6 s
      × 0.0001, 4 bands deflate 19.1 s 17.3 s 17.4 s
      Mosaic of 9 tiles, 4 bands none 7.9 s 4.4 s 3.9 s
      Mosaic of 9 tiles, 4 bands deflate 12.2 s 8.8 s 8.6 s

      Parallel work pays off most for mosaics and calculations. When a job mostly writes a large output (the 4-band case writes 1 GB of float32), the disk and compression set the pace.

      Settings for big machines and special cases:

      from earthforge import raster

raster.MAX_WORKERS = 16                         # allow up to 16 workers by default
m.save("mosaic.tif", workers=12)                # or choose for one save
m.save("mosaic.tif", workers=1)                 # one block at a time: least memory
raster.BLOCK_SIZE = 2048                        # larger blocks (multiple of 256): fewer, bigger steps

      Larger blocks (BLOCK_SIZE = 2048) use 4× more memory per block and help a little when there are very many small steps. The default of 1024 suits most cases.

      Measured peak memory

      Test raster: 8000 × 8000 px, 4 bands, uint16 (one band as float32 = 256 MB). Peak memory measured with Python's tracemalloc, with one worker (workers=1). GDAL's internal block cache is separate and not included. With the default workers, peak memory is higher (about 150–450 MB in these tests) but stays within the memory budget described above.

      Operation Peak memory Time
      raster.image(path) ~0 MB 0.1 s
      select(...), normalizedDifference(...) (no output) ~0 MB 0.0 s
      visualize(), RGB preview 66 MB 2.4 s
      visualize(palette=...), NDVI preview 50 MB 2.3 s
      normalizedDifference(...).save() 27 MB 3.2 s
      (img * 0.0001).save(), 4 bands, float32 15 MB 6.4 s
      img.select(4 bands).save(), stays uint16 14 MB 5.0 s
      img.select("B1").data 256 MB 2.3 s
      img.select("B1", "B2").data 512 MB 3.7 s

      Mosaic of the same raster cut into 9 overlapping tiles:

      Operation Peak memory Time
      raster.mosaic("tiles/") ~0 MB 0.1 s
      visualize() preview of the mosaic 66 MB 4.0 s
      mosaic.save(compress=None), uint16 22 MB 8.5 s
      mosaic.save(compress="zstd") 20 MB 9.7 s
      mosaic.clip(10 × 10 km AOI).save() 19 MB 0.3 s

      .data uses exactly the size of the result. Everything else stays small whatever the raster size. Save time grows roughly in proportion to the number of pixels written, and is usually limited by disk speed.

      Tips

      • Clip early. img.clip(aoi) before other work means every later step reads only the area of interest. This works for mosaics too.
      • Avoid .data on large images. It is the only operation whose memory grows with the image size. Use visualize() to look at the image and save() to export it.
      • Store .data if you need it twice. It is recomputed on every access: 
        arr = img.select("B8").data   # compute once
arr.mean(); arr.max()
      • Choose the compression to suit the job. compress=None is fastest to write but makes the largest files. "zstd" is fast with good compression. "deflate" is the most widely supported.
      • Keep integer data integer. Saving a plain selection, clip or mosaic keeps uint16/int16 automatically. For class maps, save(dtype="uint8") makes files much smaller.
      • Add overviews to large source files (gdaladdo or rasterio's build_overviews). visualize() then reads the small overview instead of decimating the full image, which makes previews of big rasters and mosaics much faster.
      • Use a lower max_size (for example 800) for quick looks at very large rasters. Use a higher one when you need fine detail.
      • Write to a local disk. Network drives and USB sticks are often the bottleneck for big outputs.
      • Limit GDAL's cache if needed. GDAL keeps a block cache (by default 5% of RAM). To cap it: 
        import rasterio
with rasterio.Env(GDAL_CACHEMAX=256):   # MB
    img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).save("ndvi.tif")
      PreviousPalettes & legendsNextErrors

      Errors

      The library raises short, specific exceptions. Tracebacks show your code and the message only, without the library's internal frames.

ValueError: Unknown palette 'nope'. Built-in: ['blue_red', 'change', ...]. Any matplotlib colormap also works (e.g. 'viridis', 'RdYlGn'). Run raster.showPalettes() to see them.
ValueError: colorbar_orientation must be 'vertical' or 'horizontal'
ValueError: 'labels' must be a non-empty dict like {1: 'Water', 2: 'Forest'}
ValueError: 'labels' only works with a single band (a class map).
ValueError: 'palette' has 2 colors but 'labels' has 4 classes; give one color per class.
TypeError: Give band names or numbers here (e.g. 'B8' or 8), not an Image. To show an Image, call .visualize() on it.

      Handling errors

      Because RasterNotFoundError subclasses FileNotFoundError, either one can be caught:

      from earthforge import raster, RasterNotFoundError

try:
    img = raster.image("missing.tif")
except RasterNotFoundError as e:
    print(e)

      The errors are still ordinary ValueError, TypeError, RasterNotFoundError and RasterReadError instances, so except ValueError: and similar work as usual.

      A note on SyntaxError

      A SyntaxError is raised by Python itself, before any library code runs, so its message can't be improved by the library. The most common case:

      ndvi.gt(0.2).and(ndvi.lte(0.3))     # SyntaxError: `and` is a Python keyword
ndvi.gt(0.2).And(ndvi.lte(0.3))     # correct
ndvi.gt(0.2).and_(ndvi.lte(0.3))    # also correct (lowercase spelling)
(ndvi > 0.2) & (ndvi <= 0.3)        # also correct (operators)

      Debugging the library

      To see the library's internal frames in tracebacks (useful when reporting a bug):

      import earthforge
earthforge.FULL_TRACEBACKS = True

      Errors that come from other packages (numpy, rasterio, matplotlib) always keep their full traceback.

      PreviousMemory & performanceNextNumber helpers

      User guide

      Arithmetic helpers

      from earthforge import add, subtract

      add(a, b)

      Returns a + b.

      add(3, 4)      # 7

      subtract(a, b)

      Returns a - b.

      subtract(10, 5)   # 5

      Both functions work with any values that support + / -, including numbers and NumPy arrays:

      from earthforge import raster, subtract
img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif")
diff = subtract(img.select("B8").data, img.select("B4").data)   # NIR - Red, as an array
      PreviousErrorsNextAPI reference

      API reference

      Generated automatically from the docstrings in earthforge/raster.py, earthforge/vector.py, earthforge/cluster.py and earthforge/pca.py. For explanations and examples, see the user guide pages.

      raster

      Functions

      image()

      raster.image(path)
      Opens a raster file as a lazy Image. Only the metadata is read.

Parameters
----------
path : str or Path
    Path to a GeoTIFF, or any format rasterio can read.

Returns
-------
Image

Raises
------
RasterNotFoundError
    If the file does not exist.
RasterReadError
    If the file exists but cannot be read as a raster.

Examples
--------
>>> img = raster.image("sampleImage1.tif")

      mosaic()

      raster.mosaic(images, method='last', res=None, save=False)
      Mosaics several rasters into one image, without loading them into memory.

Works like a GDAL virtual raster (VRT): nothing is read when the mosaic is
created. When you visualize it, a small preview is read; when you save it,
it is written block by block (1024 x 1024 pixels), and each block reads
only the overlapping part of each source. Memory use therefore depends on
the block size, not on the size of the inputs, so very large mosaics work
on ordinary PCs. Saving shows a progress bar.

Parameters
----------
images : list, str or Path
    The rasters to combine:

    - a list of Images and/or file paths
    - a folder (all .tif / .tiff files in it)
    - a glob pattern, e.g. "tiles/*.tif" or "scenes/**/B04.tif"

    All must have the same CRS and the same number of bands. They may be
    computed images (e.g. NDVI of each scene) and may overlap.
method : str, default "last"
    How overlapping pixels are combined: "last" (later images on top),
    "first" (earlier images on top), "min", "max" or "mean".
    NoData pixels never cover valid ones.
res : float or (float, float), optional
    Pixel size of the mosaic. Default: the first image's pixel size.
    Images with another pixel size are resampled (nearest neighbour).
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "mosaic_mosaic_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image
    Covers the union of all inputs; band names come from the first image.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If no rasters are found, CRSs or band counts differ, or `method` /
    `res` are invalid.

Examples
--------
>>> m = raster.mosaic(["tile_1.tif", "tile_2.tif", "tile_3.tif"])
>>> m = raster.mosaic("tiles/")                          # every .tif in a folder
>>> m = raster.mosaic("tiles/*.tif", method="max")
>>> m.select("B4", "B3", "B2").visualize(min=0, max=3000)
>>> m.save("mosaic.tif")                                 # streamed, with a progress bar
>>> ndvis = [raster.image(p).normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]) for p in paths]
>>> raster.mosaic(ndvis, method="max", save="max_ndvi.tif")

      stack()

      raster.stack(images, names=None, save=False)
      Stacks the bands of several images into one multi-band image.

Useful for combining single-band files (e.g. one GeoTIFF per band) into
one image. Nothing is read until you visualize or save the result.

The first image sets the grid (extent and pixel size). Images on a
different grid, e.g. 20 m bands stacked onto 10 m bands, are resampled
to it (nearest neighbour); areas they don't cover become NoData.

Parameters
----------
images : list, str or Path
    A list of Images and/or file paths, a folder (all .tif / .tiff files,
    in name order) or a glob pattern such as "bands/*_B0[2348].tif".
    All must have the same CRS.
names : list of str, optional
    New band names, one per band of the result. Default: the original
    band names; where names repeat, they are prefixed with the file name.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "stack_stack_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image

Raises
------
ValueError
    If no images are given, CRSs differ, or `names` has the wrong length.

Examples
--------
>>> s = raster.stack(["B02.tif", "B03.tif", "B04.tif", "B08.tif"],
...                  names=["blue", "green", "red", "nir"])
>>> s = raster.stack("bands/")
>>> s = raster.stack([img.select("B8"), ndvi.rename("NDVI")], save="nir_ndvi.tif")

      palettes()

      raster.palettes()
      Lists the built-in palettes.

Any matplotlib colormap name (e.g. "viridis", "RdYlGn") also works as a palette.
Add "_r" to any name to reverse it, e.g. "ndvi_r".

Returns

Examples

>>> raster.palettes()
['blue_red', 'change', 'diverging', 'elevation', 'evi', 'nbr', ...]
>>> "ndvi" in raster.palettes()
True

      Classes

      Image

      class Image
      A lazy raster image: operations build a recipe, and pixels are read only when needed.

Create one with `raster.image(path)`.

      bounds()

      bounds(save=False)
      Returns the image's bounding box, and optionally saves it as GeoJSON.

Parameters
----------
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves the bounding box as a rectangle to
    "<image>_bounds_<epoch>.geojson" in the current folder; a string
    saves to that path (GeoJSON for .geojson / .json; other vector
    formats such as .shp or .kml also work). GeoJSON is written in
    EPSG:4326 (longitude/latitude).

Returns
-------
BoundingBox
    (left, bottom, right, top) in the image's CRS. Read the values as
    ``b.left``, ``b.bottom``, ``b.right``, ``b.top``.

Examples
--------
>>> extent = evi.bounds()
>>> extent.left, extent.top
>>> extent = evi.bounds(save=True)              # also writes a .geojson
>>> extent = evi.bounds(save="evi_extent.geojson")

      res property

      The pixel size (x, y), in CRS units.

Degrees for a geographic CRS such as EPSG:4326, metres for UTM.

Examples
--------
>>> img.res
(8.983152841195215e-05, 8.983152841195215e-05)
>>> xres, yres = raster.image("utm_scene.tif").res      # e.g. (10.0, 10.0) metres

      data property

      All pixels at full resolution, as a float32 numpy array (bands, rows, cols).

Computed every time it is accessed, and uses the most memory of any
operation. Store it in a variable if you need it more than once
(``arr = img.data``). For large images prefer visualize() (preview)
or save() (streamed). NoData pixels are NaN.

Examples
--------
>>> arr = img.select("B8").data          # compute once, keep the array
>>> arr.shape
(1, 551, 763)
>>> float(np.nanmean(arr))               # average NIR value

      bandNames()

      bandNames()
      Returns the band names, in band order.

Returns
-------
BandList
    A list of names, with ``.size()`` (number of bands) and ``.get(i)``.

Examples
--------
>>> img.bandNames()
['B1', 'B2', 'B3', ...]
>>> img.bandNames().size()

      select()

      select(*bands)
      Selects bands, returning a new image that contains only those bands.

No pixels are read or copied; the new image just points at the chosen bands.

Parameters
----------
*bands : str, int, or a list of them
    Band names (e.g. "B4") or 1-based band numbers (e.g. 4), separately
    or as one list. The new image keeps the order you give.

Returns
-------
Image

Raises
------
ValueError
    If no bands are given, or a band does not exist.

Examples
--------
>>> nir = img.select("B8")
>>> rgb = img.select("B4", "B3", "B2")
>>> rgb = img.select(["B4", "B3", "B2"])
>>> rgb = img.select([4, 3, 2])

      rename()

      rename(*names)
      Renames the bands, returning a new image.

Parameters
----------
*names : str, or a list of str
    One new name per band, in band order.

Returns
-------
Image

Raises
------
ValueError
    If the number of names doesn't match the number of bands.

Examples
--------
>>> ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI")
>>> img.select("B4", "B3").rename(["red", "green"])

      lt()

      lt(other, save=False)
      Tests whether the image is less than `other`.

Returns 1 where true and 0 where false (NaN on NoData).

--------
>>> water = ndvi.lt(0)                       # or ndvi < 0
>>> darker = img.select("B4").lt(img.select("B3"))

      lte(other, save=False)
      Tests whether the image is less than or equal to `other`.

Returns 1 where true and 0 where false (NaN on NoData).
Operator form: ``img <= other``. `save` works as in add().

Examples
--------
>>> sparse = ndvi.lte(0.3)                   # or ndvi <= 0.3

      gt()

      gt(other, save=False)
      Tests whether the image is greater than `other`.

Returns 1 where true and 0 where false (NaN on NoData).
Operator form: ``img > other``. `save` works as in add().

Examples
--------
>>> vegetation = ndvi.gt(0.3)                # or ndvi > 0.3
>>> share = ndvi.gt(0.3).data.mean()         # fraction of vegetated pixels

      gte()

      gte(other, save=False)
      Tests whether the image is greater than or equal to `other`.

Returns 1 where true and 0 where false (NaN on NoData).
Operator form: ``img >= other``. `save` works as in add().

Examples
--------
>>> dense = ndvi.gte(0.6)                    # or ndvi >= 0.6

      eq()

      eq(other, save=False)
      Tests whether the image is equal to `other`, e.g. to pick a class.

Returns 1 where true and 0 where false (NaN on NoData). There is no
``==`` operator form, so images keep working in lists and dicts.

Parameters
----------
other : Image, number, or list of numbers
    A list picks several values at once: 1 where the pixel equals ANY of them.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_eq_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image

Examples
--------
>>> dense = classified.eq(4)            # 1 where class 4, else 0
>>> veg = classified.eq([3, 4])         # 1 where class 3 or 4

      neq()

      neq(other, save=False)
      Tests whether the image is not equal to `other`.

Returns 1 where true and 0 where false (NaN on NoData). There is no
``!=`` operator form. A list gives 1 where the pixel equals NONE of
the values. `save` works as in add().

Examples
--------
>>> not_water = classified.neq(1)
>>> land = classified.neq([0, 1])            # neither class 0 nor class 1

      selectClasses()

      selectClasses(classes, save=False)
      Selects one or more classes: keeps those pixel values, all others become NoData.

Parameters
----------
classes : number or list of numbers

save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_selectClasses_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image
    Same values for the chosen classes, NaN (NoData) everywhere else.

Examples
--------
>>> water = classified.selectClasses(1)
>>> vegetation = classified.selectClasses([3, 4])

      mergeClasses()

      mergeClasses(classes, into=None, save=False)
      Merges two or more classes into one class value.

Pixels of the other classes are left unchanged.

Parameters
----------
classes : list of numbers, or dict
    The class values to merge, together with `into`. Or a dict
    ``{new_value: [old_values]}`` to do several merges at once
    (then leave out `into`).
into : number, optional
    The value the merged classes get. Required unless `classes` is a dict.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_mergeClasses_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image

Raises
------
ValueError
    If `into` is missing, or the same class is listed in two groups.

Examples
--------
>>> merged = classified.mergeClasses([1, 2], into=1)
>>> merged = classified.mergeClasses({1: [1, 2], 2: [3, 4]})   # 4 classes -> 2

      updateMask(mask, save=False)

Parameters
----------
mask : Image

      geometry()

      geometry()
      Returns the image extent (footprint) as a Vector with one polygon.

The polygon is in the image's CRS. Print it, inspect it with .meta(),
or export it, e.g. ``img.geometry().save("extent.geojson")``.

Returns
-------
vector.Vector

Examples
--------
>>> extent = img.geometry()
>>> print(extent)
>>> extent.toGeoJSON()
>>> extent.save("extent.geojson")

      clip()

      clip(geometry, save=False)
      Clips the image to a vector: crops to its extent and masks pixels outside it.

Pixels outside the shapes become NoData. The result is also cropped to
the vector's bounding box, so it is smaller, faster and uses less memory.
The vector is reprojected to the image's CRS automatically.

Parameters
----------
geometry : vector.Vector
    e.g. ``vector.Open("boundary.shp")`` or another image's ``.geometry()``.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_clip_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `geometry` is not a Vector.
ValueError
    If the vector has no geometries or no CRS, or does not overlap the image.

Examples
--------
>>> from earthforge import raster, vector
>>> aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
>>> clipped = img.clip(aoi)
>>> img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).clip(aoi, save="ndvi_aoi.tif")

      And()

      And(other, save=False)
      Calculates the logical AND of the image and `other`.

Returns 1 where both are non-zero and 0 elsewhere (NaN on NoData).
Operator form: ``a & b``. Capitalized because `and` is a Python keyword.
`save` works as in add().

Examples
--------
>>> moderate = ndvi.gt(0.34).And(ndvi.lt(0.5))
>>> moderate = (ndvi > 0.34) & (ndvi < 0.5)

      Or()

      Or(other, save=False)
      Calculates the logical OR of the image and `other`.

Returns 1 where either is non-zero and 0 elsewhere (NaN on NoData).
Operator form: ``a | b``. `save` works as in add().

Examples
--------
>>> extreme = ndvi.lt(0).Or(ndvi.gt(0.8))
>>> extreme = (ndvi < 0) | (ndvi > 0.8)      # same, with operators

      Not()

      Not(save=False)
      Calculates the logical NOT of the image.

Returns 1 where the image is 0 and 0 elsewhere (NaN on NoData).
Operator form: ``~img``. `save` works as in add().

Examples
--------
>>> land = ndvi.lt(0).Not()                  # everything that isn't water
>>> land = ~(ndvi < 0)                       # same, with operators

      and_()

      and_(other, save=False)

      Same as And().

      or_()

      or_(other, save=False)

      Same as Or().

      not_()

      not_(save=False)

      Same as Not().

      where()

      where(*rules, otherwise=None, save=False)
      Reclassifies a raster: replaces pixel values wherever a condition is true.

Rules are applied in order, so where rules overlap the last matching
rule wins (the same as chaining several .where() calls).

Parameters
----------
*rules : (test, value) pairs
    `test` is an Image (a condition such as ndvi.lt(0.1)); pixels where it
    is non-zero get `value` (a number or an Image). Accepted forms:

    - ``where(test, value)``                         one rule
    - ``where((test1, 1), (test2, 2), ...)``         several tuples
    - ``where([(test1, 1), (test2, 2)])``            a list of tuples
    - ``where({test1: 1, test2: 2})``                a dict (keeps order)
    - ``where({test1, 1}, {test2, 2})``              2-item sets, when the
      value is a number (sets have no order, so the Image is taken as
      the test and the number as the value)
otherwise : number, optional
    Value for pixels that match no rule. Default: keep the original value.
    Use e.g. ``otherwise=0`` for a clean class map.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_where_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image
    Same band names as this image. NoData pixels in a test never match.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If no rules are given, a rule is malformed, or band counts don't match.
TypeError
    If a test is not an Image, or a value / `otherwise` is not a number or Image.

Examples
--------
>>> ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI")
>>> classes = ndvi.where(
...     (ndvi.lt(0.1), 1),                          # water / bare
...     (ndvi.gte(0.1).And(ndvi.lt(0.34)), 2),      # sparse vegetation
...     (ndvi.gte(0.34).And(ndvi.lt(0.5)), 3),      # moderate vegetation
...     (ndvi.gte(0.5), 4),                         # dense vegetation
...     otherwise=0,
... ).rename("class")
>>> classes.visualize(labels={1: "Water", 2: "Sparse", 3: "Moderate", 4: "Dense"},
...                   palette=["0000FF", "D2B48C", "9ACD32", "006400"])
>>> ndvi.where(ndvi.lt(0), 0)                       # clip negatives to 0
>>> ndvi.where({ndvi < 0.1: 1, ndvi >= 0.5: 2}, otherwise=0)

      remap()

      remap(from_values, to_values=None, default=None, save=False)
      Remaps pixel values: replaces each listed value with a new value.

Useful for recoding class maps, e.g. merging classes or converting
codes from one classification scheme to another. Values are matched
exactly, so it is meant for class / integer values. Every listed value
is matched against the ORIGINAL pixel values, so a chain like 1 -> 2,
2 -> 3 does not turn 1 into 3.

Parameters
----------
from_values : list of numbers, or dict
    The values to replace. Or a dict {old: new} (then leave `to_values` out).
to_values : list of numbers, optional
    The new values, one for each entry in `from_values`.
default : number, optional
    Value for pixels whose value is not listed. Default: keep their
    original value. Use ``default=float("nan")`` to turn them into NoData.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_remap_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image
    Same band names as this image. Applied to every band. NoData stays NoData.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If the lists are empty or have different lengths, or a value is not a number.
TypeError
    If `default` is not a number.

Examples
--------
>>> merged = classes.remap([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 1, 2, 2])          # 4 classes -> 2
>>> merged = classes.remap({1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 2, 4: 2})            # same, as a dict
>>> veg = classes.remap([3, 4], [1, 1], default=0)               # binary mask
>>> only_water = classes.remap([1], [1], default=float("nan"))   # others -> NoData

      expression()

      expression(expression, map=None, save=False)
      Evaluates a mathematical expression on the image's bands.

The text is parsed safely; it is never run as Python code.

Parameters
----------
expression : str
    The formula. It can use:

    - names from `map`, and this image's band names directly (e.g. ``B8``)
    - ``b('B8')`` (by name) or ``b(7)`` (0-based index)
    - numbers, ``+ - * / **``, ``( )``
    - comparisons ``< <= > >= == !=`` (give 1 / 0)
    - logic ``&&`` ``||`` ``!`` or ``and`` ``or`` ``not``
    - functions ``abs sqrt log log10 exp``
map : dict, optional
    Variable name -> Image or number, e.g. {"NIR": img.select("B8")}.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_expression_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image
    Band names follow the band-math rules (the left-most image's names);
    use .rename() to name the result.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If the formula is invalid, uses unsupported syntax or unknown names,
    or contains no band or image.
TypeError
    If a `map` value is not an Image or a number.

Examples
--------
>>> evi = img.expression(
...     "2.5 * ((NIR - RED) / (NIR + 6 * RED - 7.5 * BLUE + 1))",
...     {"NIR": img.select("B8").multiply(0.0001),
...      "RED": img.select("B4").multiply(0.0001),
...      "BLUE": img.select("B2").multiply(0.0001)},
... ).rename("EVI")
>>> ndvi = img.expression("(B8 - B4) / (B8 + B4)")
>>> water = img.expression("b('B3') > b('B8') && B8 < 1500")

      Expression()

      Expression(expression, map=None, save=False)

      Same as expression().

      normalizedDifference()

      normalizedDifference(bandNames=None, save=False)
      Calculates the Normalized Difference between two bands.

Computes ``(first - second) / (first + second)`` for every pixel. This
is the formula behind NDVI, NDWI, NDBI, NBR, NDSI and similar indices.
Pixels where the sum is 0 become NaN.

Parameters
----------
bandNames : list of 2 band names or numbers, optional
    The two bands, in order, e.g. ["B8", "B4"] for NDVI.
    Default: the first two bands of the image.
save : bool or str, default False
    True saves "<image>_nd_<epoch>.tif"; a string saves to that path.

Returns
-------
Image
    A single-band image named "nd", with values from -1 to 1.
    Use .rename() to give it a meaningful name.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If `bandNames` does not contain exactly 2 bands, a band does not
    exist, or the image has fewer than 2 bands.

Examples
--------
>>> ndvi = img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"])      # vegetation
>>> ndwi = img.normalizedDifference(["B3", "B8"])      # water
>>> ndbi = img.normalizedDifference(["B11", "B8"])     # built-up
>>> img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"], save="ndvi.tif")

      sample()

      sample(numPixels=5000, seed=0, geometries=True, progress=True, region=None)
      Samples random pixels and returns their band values as a dataset (one row per pixel).

Reads as little as possible: when the samples are spread thinly over a
large image (e.g. 5,000 pixels on a huge mosaic), only small 256 x 256
pieces around the sampled pixels are read instead of whole blocks.
Memory use stays small. Pixels with NoData in any band are left out, so
the result can have fewer rows than asked.

Parameters
----------
numPixels : int, default 5000
    Number of random pixels to sample.
seed : int, default 0
    Random seed: the same seed gives the same pixels.
geometries : bool, default True
    Add a point (the pixel centre) to each row. False gives a plain table.
progress : bool, default True
    Show a progress bar for large images.
region : vector.Vector, optional
    Only sample pixels whose centre is inside these shapes (e.g. a
    boundary). Reprojected to the image's CRS automatically. The full
    `numPixels` are drawn inside the region when it has that many pixels.

Returns
-------
vector.Vector
    One column per band, plus point geometries in the image's CRS.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If numPixels is not a positive whole number, or the region doesn't
    overlap the image.
TypeError
    If `region` is not a Vector.

Examples
--------
>>> samples = img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8").sample(2000)
>>> samples.show(5)
>>> samples.save("training_pixels.csv")
>>> aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
>>> inside = img.sample(1000, region=aoi)            # only inside the boundary
>>> cluster.kMeans(5).train(samples)

      cluster()

      cluster(clusterer, outputName='cluster', numPixels=5000, seed=0, region=None)
      Assigns every pixel to a cluster.

Give a trained clusterer (``cluster.wekaKMeans(5).train(img)``), or an
untrained one (``cluster.wekaKMeans(5)``) to train it on this image
right away. The result is a lazy single-band image of cluster numbers
(0, 1, 2, ...). Pixels with NoData in any input band stay NoData.
Saved files are uint8 (cluster numbers) with NoData = 255.

Parameters
----------
clusterer : cluster.TrainedClusterer or cluster.Clusterer
    A trained clusterer, or an untrained one to train on this image.
outputName : str, default "cluster"
    Name of the output band.
numPixels : int, default 5000
    Pixels sampled for training, when `clusterer` is not trained yet.
seed : int, default 0
    Random seed for the training sample.
region : vector.Vector, optional
    When `clusterer` is not trained yet: train only on pixels inside
    these shapes. The whole image is still clustered.

Returns
-------
Image

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `clusterer` is not a clusterer.
ValueError
    If the image lacks a band the clusterer was trained on.

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)
>>> clusters = img.cluster(trained)
>>> clusters.visualize(labels={i: f"Cluster {i}" for i in range(5)})
>>> clusters.save("clusters.tif")
>>> quick = img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5))                     # train and apply in one step
>>> local = img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5), region=aoi)         # trained inside aoi only

      pca()

      pca(model, numPixels=10000, standardize=False, seed=0, region=None)
      Transforms the image into principal components (bands PC1, PC2, ...).

Give a trained PCA (``pca.PCA(3).train(img)``), or a number of
components to train one on this image right away. The result is lazy:
visualizing reads a preview and saving streams it block by block.

Parameters
----------
model : pca.TrainedPCA, int or None
    A trained PCA, or the number of components to keep (None = all).
numPixels : int, default 10000
    Pixels sampled for training, when `model` is a number.
standardize : bool, default False
    Scale bands to unit variance before training, when `model` is a number.
seed : int, default 0
    Random seed for the training sample.
region : vector.Vector, optional
    When `model` is a number: learn the components only from pixels
    inside these shapes. The whole image is still transformed.

Returns
-------
Image
    Float32 bands named PC1, PC2, ...

Examples
--------
>>> model = pca.PCA(3).train(img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11", "B12"))
>>> model.info()
>>> pcs = img.pca(model)
>>> pcs.visualize(bands=["PC1", "PC2", "PC3"])
>>> quick = img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8").pca(2)        # train and apply in one step
>>> local = img.pca(3, region=aoi)                         # components learned inside aoi

      save()

      save(path=None, compress='deflate', dtype=None, nodata=None, progress=True, workers=None, _label=None)
      Saves the image as a GeoTIFF, streaming it block by block.

The image is computed and written in 1024 x 1024 pixel blocks, one band
at a time, so memory use stays small (a few MB per band) however large
the image is. On a computer with several CPU cores, blocks are computed
in parallel. Band names are written into the file, compression uses
all CPU cores, and a progress bar shows how far it is.

Parameters
----------
path : str, optional
    Output file. Default: "<image name>_<band names>_<epoch time>.tif"
    in the current folder.
compress : str or None, default "deflate"
    "deflate" (smaller, widely supported), "zstd" (a bit faster),
    "lzw" (fastest compression, larger file), or None (no compression:
    fastest, largest file).
dtype : str, optional
    Data type of the file, e.g. "uint16", "int16", "float32".
    Default: the source's integer type when pixel values are passed
    through unchanged (select, clip, mosaic, ...), otherwise "float32".
    Saving computed values to an integer type rounds them and clips
    them to the type's range.
nodata : number, optional
    Value written for NoData pixels. Default: NaN for float types; for
    integer types the source's NoData value, or 0.
progress : bool, default True
    Show a progress bar.
workers : int, optional
    How many blocks are computed at the same time (threads).
    Default: one per CPU core, up to 8 (see raster.MAX_WORKERS).
    Fewer are used if the blocks in progress would need more than about
    a quarter of the free memory. Use 1 to process one block at a time.

Returns
-------
str
    The absolute path of the saved file.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If `path` is one of the files this image reads from, or `dtype` /
    `nodata` are invalid.

Examples
--------
>>> img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).rename("NDVI").save("ndvi.tif")
>>> img.select("B4", "B3", "B2").save()
>>> mosaic.save("mosaic.tif", compress="zstd")

      meta()

      meta()
      Prints a summary of the image and returns its metadata. Reads no pixels.

Shows the size, number of bands, band names, data type, NoData value,
CRS, resolution, bounds and transform.

Returns
-------
dict
    driver, dtype, nodata, width, height, count, crs, transform, bandNames
    (and sources, for a mosaic).

Examples
--------
>>> img.meta()                               # print the summary
>>> m = img.meta()
>>> m["crs"], m["count"]
(CRS.from_epsg(4326), 26)

      visualize()

      visualize(bands=None, min=None, max=None, gamma=1.0, palette=None, colorbar=True, colorbar_label=None, colorbar_orientation='vertical', labels=None, overlay=None, overlay_color='red', max_size=1500, save_chart=False, dpi=200)
      Displays the image as a map chart.

Each band is stretched linearly from `min` to `max`, then gamma
correction is applied. Shows an RGB composite (3 bands), a single band
with a palette and colorbar, or a class map with a legend (`labels`).
Only a downsampled preview is read (see `max_size`), so this is fast
and light on memory even for large images.

Parameters
----------
bands : str, int, or list, optional
    1 band  -> single-band view, colored with `palette` + a colorbar.
    3 bands -> RGB composite, in the order [red, green, blue].
    Band names (e.g. ["B4", "B3", "B2"]) or 1-based numbers ([4, 3, 2]).
    Default: the first three bands, or the first band if fewer than 3.
min : float or list of float, optional
    Value shown as the lowest color. One number for all bands, or one
    per band. Default: each band's 2nd percentile.
max : float or list of float, optional
    Value shown as the highest color. Default: each band's 98th percentile.
gamma : float or list of float, default 1.0
    Gamma correction. Above 1 brightens, below 1 darkens.
palette : str or list of colors, optional  (single band only)
    - a built-in palette: "ndvi", "ndwi", "evi", "ndbi", "nbr", "ndsi",
      "elevation", "temperature", "precipitation", "water", ... (see raster.palettes())
    - any matplotlib colormap: "viridis", "RdYlGn", "Spectral", "terrain", ...
    - add "_r" to reverse any of them, e.g. "ndvi_r"
    - or a list of colors: ["0000FF", "FFFFFF", "008000"] (hex with or without '#')
    Default: "gray". Run raster.showPalettes() to see them all.
colorbar : bool, default True  (single band only)
    Show a colorbar with the real pixel values.
colorbar_label : str, optional
    Colorbar title. Default: the band name.
colorbar_orientation : "vertical" or "horizontal", default "vertical"
labels : dict, optional  (single band only)
    For class maps (e.g. the output of where()): {value: "name"}.
    Draws one flat color per class and a legend instead of a colorbar.
    Colors come from `palette`: a list with one color per class, or a
    palette name to sample from (default "tab10"). Pixels whose value
    is not in `labels` are transparent. `min`/`max`/`gamma` are ignored.
overlay : vector.Vector or list of Vectors, optional
    Vectors drawn on top of the image as outlines (polygons), lines or
    dots (points), e.g. a boundary or sample points. They are
    reprojected to the image's CRS. The map keeps the image's extent.
overlay_color : str or list of str, default "red"
    Color of the overlay; a list gives one color per overlay vector.
max_size : int, default 1500
    Longest side, in pixels, of the preview that is read and drawn.
    Larger = more detail but more RAM. Images smaller than this are shown
    at full resolution.
save_chart : bool, default False
    Also save the chart as "<image name>_<epoch time>.png" in the current folder.
dpi : int, default 200
    Resolution of the saved PNG. Only used when save_chart=True.

Returns
-------
str or None
    The saved PNG file name when save_chart=True, otherwise None.

Examples
--------
>>> img.visualize(bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], min=1000, max=4000, gamma=1.2)
>>> img.normalizedDifference(["B8", "B4"]).visualize(min=-0.2, max=0.8, palette="ndvi")
>>> img.select("B8").visualize(palette="viridis", colorbar_orientation="horizontal")
>>> classes.visualize(labels={1: "Water", 2: "Sparse", 3: "Moderate", 4: "Dense"},
...                   palette=["0000FF", "D2B48C", "9ACD32", "006400"])
>>> img.visualize(bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], min=1000, max=4000, overlay=aoi)
>>> img.visualize(bands=[4, 3, 2], save_chart=True, dpi=300)

      Exceptions

      RasterNotFoundError

      class RasterNotFoundError(FileNotFoundError)
      Raised when the raster path does not exist.

      RasterReadError

      Raised when the file exists but cannot be read as a raster.

      vector

      Functions

      Open()

      vector.Open(path, layer=None, x=None, y=None, crs=None)
      Opens a vector file or table as a Vector.

Supported: Shapefile (.shp), GeoJSON (.geojson/.json), KML (.kml), KMZ (.kmz),
GeoPackage (.gpkg), Parquet / GeoParquet (.parquet), CSV (.csv) and
Excel (.xlsx/.xls, any sheet).

Tables (CSV, Excel, plain Parquet) become point features when they have
coordinate columns (e.g. longitude/latitude, lon/lat, x/y) or a WKT
geometry column; otherwise they are opened as a plain table.

Parameters
----------
path : str or Path
    The file to open.
layer : str or int, optional
    Layer of a multi-layer file (GeoPackage, KML folders), or sheet of an
    Excel file, by name or 0-based index. Default: the first layer/sheet;
    for KML/KMZ, all layers are combined. List them with vector.layers(path).
x, y : str, optional
    Column names with point coordinates in a table. Default: detected
    automatically.
crs : str or int, optional
    CRS of the data when the file doesn't define one, e.g. "EPSG:32643".
    Tables with longitude/latitude columns default to EPSG:4326.

Returns
-------
Vector

Raises
------
VectorNotFoundError
    If the file does not exist.
VectorReadError
    If the format is not supported or the file can't be read.

Examples
--------
>>> aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
>>> pts = vector.Open("stations.csv")                       # lon/lat columns -> points
>>> sheet = vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer="2024")         # a specific sheet
>>> kml = vector.Open("sites.kmz")

      layers()

      vector.layers(path)
      Lists the layers of a vector file, or the sheets of an Excel file.

Parameters
----------
path : str or Path

Returns
-------
list of str

Examples
--------
>>> vector.layers("survey.xlsx")
['2023', '2024']

      fromGeometry()

      vector.fromGeometry(geometry, crs='EPSG:4326', properties=None)
      Creates a Vector from your own geometry or geometries.

Accepts shapely geometries, GeoJSON (a geometry, a Feature or a whole
FeatureCollection, e.g. drawn on geojson.io), WKT text, or a list of
(x, y) corners for a polygon. Give a list to create several features.

Parameters
----------
geometry : geometry, dict, str, list
    One geometry, or a list of geometries.
crs : str or int, default "EPSG:4326"
    CRS of the coordinates. EPSG:4326 means longitude/latitude in degrees.
properties : dict or list of dict, optional
    Columns for the features: a dict of lists ({"name": ["A", "B"]}), or
    one dict per feature.

Returns
-------
Vector

Raises
------
ValueError, TypeError
    If a geometry can't be read.

Examples
--------
>>> aoi = vector.fromGeometry({"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[73.11, 33.69], [73.14, 33.69],
...                                                                [73.14, 33.71], [73.11, 33.71], [73.11, 33.69]]]})
>>> aoi = vector.fromGeometry("POLYGON ((73.11 33.69, 73.14 33.69, 73.14 33.71, 73.11 33.69))")
>>> fields = vector.fromGeometry([field_1, field_2], properties={"name": ["north", "south"]})
>>> img.sample(1000, region=aoi)

      Rectangle()

      vector.Rectangle(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax, crs='EPSG:4326')
      Creates a rectangle from its corner coordinates, as a Vector with one feature.

Parameters
----------
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax : float
    West, south, east and north edges (longitude/latitude for EPSG:4326).
crs : str or int, default "EPSG:4326"
    CRS of the coordinates.

Returns
-------
Vector

Raises
------
ValueError
    If xmin >= xmax or ymin >= ymax.

Examples
--------
>>> box = vector.Rectangle(73.11, 33.69, 73.14, 33.71)              # lon/lat
>>> box = vector.Rectangle(330000, 3700000, 340000, 3710000, crs="EPSG:32643")   # UTM metres
>>> img.sample(1000, region=box)

      Polygon()

      vector.Polygon(coordinates, crs='EPSG:4326')
      Creates a polygon from a list of (x, y) corners, as a Vector with one feature.

The polygon is closed automatically (the last corner joins the first).

Parameters
----------
coordinates : list of (x, y)
    At least 3 corners (longitude, latitude for EPSG:4326).
crs : str or int, default "EPSG:4326"
    CRS of the coordinates.

Returns
-------
Vector

Raises
------
ValueError
    If there are fewer than 3 corners or the shape is invalid.

Examples
--------
>>> lake = vector.Polygon([(73.110, 33.690), (73.145, 33.692), (73.148, 33.716), (73.118, 33.712)])
>>> pca.PCA(3).train(img, region=lake)

      Point()

      vector.Point(x, y, crs='EPSG:4326')
      Creates a point, as a Vector with one feature. Use .buffer(metres) to make a circle around it.

Parameters
----------
x, y : float
    Coordinates (longitude, latitude for EPSG:4326).
crs : str or int, default "EPSG:4326"
    CRS of the coordinates.

Returns
-------
Vector

Examples
--------
>>> site = vector.Point(73.125, 33.700)
>>> circle = site.buffer(500)                    # 500 m around the point
>>> img.sample(300, region=circle)

      Classes

      Vector

      class Vector
      A vector dataset (features with geometry and attributes) or a plain table.

Create one with `vector.Open(path)`. A raster's extent is also a Vector:
`img.geometry()`.

      data property

      The features as a geopandas GeoDataFrame (a pandas DataFrame for tables without geometry).

Use it for anything geopandas or pandas can do: filtering rows,
statistics, joins, plotting.

>>> aoi.data.head()
>>> lake = aoi.data[aoi.data["name"] == "lake"]
>>> aoi.data.to_crs(32643).area.sum()        # total area in m² (UTM)
