      show()

      show(n=10, columns=None)
      Shows records as a table: the first `n`, or all of them.

In Jupyter the table is displayed as a formatted table; elsewhere it is
printed. Geometries are shown as short WKT text.

Parameters
----------
n : int or "all", default 10
    How many records to show from the top. "all" (or None) shows every record.
columns : list of str, optional
    Only show these columns.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If `n` is not a positive number or "all", or a column doesn't exist.

Examples
--------
>>> stations.show()                                  # first 10 records
>>> stations.show(25)                                # first 25
>>> stations.show("all")                             # every record
>>> stations.show(5, columns=["station_id", "district", "rain_mm"])

      get()

      get(key)
      Returns a column's values, or one feature.

Parameters
----------
key : str or int
    A column name: returns that column's values as a list.
    A position (0-based, negative counts from the end): returns that
    feature as a Feature.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If the column doesn't exist or the position is out of range.

Examples
--------
>>> rain = stations.get("rain_mm")           # list of 600 values
>>> max(rain)
>>> first = stations.get(0)                  # a Feature
>>> first.get("district")
'North'
>>> stations.get(-1)                         # the last feature

      first()

      first()
      Returns the first feature, as a Feature.

Examples
--------
>>> stations.first().properties()

      map()

      map(func)
      Runs a function on every feature and builds a new dataset from the results.

Your function receives one Feature and returns a Feature, usually made
with ``f.set({...})`` (same geometry, new or changed properties) or
``vector.Feature(geometry, {...})`` (new geometry). Return None to drop
the feature. This is how custom columns are added.

Parameters
----------
func : function
    Takes a Feature, returns a Feature (or None to drop it).

Returns
-------
Vector

Raises
------
TypeError
    If the function returns something other than a Feature or None.

Examples
--------
>>> def add_columns(f):
...     return f.set({
...         "rain_cm": f.get("rain_mm") / 10,
...         "wet": f.get("rain_mm") > 20,
...     })
>>> stations2 = stations.map(add_columns)
>>> districts.map(lambda f: f.set({"area_km2": f.area() / 1e6}))
>>> districts.map(lambda f: vector.Feature(f.centroid(), {"district": f.get("district")}))

      filter()

      filter(filter)
      Keeps the features that pass a filter.

Parameters
----------
filter : Filter
    Built with Filter.eq / gt / inList / rangeContains / stringContains / ...
    and combined with ``&``, ``|``, ``~``.

Returns
-------
Vector

Examples
--------
>>> from earthforge.vector import Filter
>>> wet = stations.filter(Filter.gt("rain_mm", 20))
>>> stations.filter(Filter.eq("district", "North") & Filter.gte("ndvi", 0.4)).size()

      filterBounds()

      filterBounds(geometry)
      Keeps the features that intersect a geometry (spatial filter).

Parameters
----------
geometry : Vector or Image
    Features touching any of its shapes are kept. For an Image, its
    extent is used. Reprojected to this dataset's CRS automatically.

Returns
-------
Vector

Examples
--------
>>> in_aoi = stations.filterBounds(aoi)
>>> on_image = stations.filterBounds(img)            # inside the image's extent

      sort()

      sort(column, ascending=True)
      Sorts the features by a column.

Examples
--------
>>> stations.sort("rain_mm", ascending=False).show(5)     # 5 wettest

      limit()

      limit(n, column=None, ascending=True)
      Keeps the first `n` features, optionally after sorting by a column.

Examples
--------
>>> stations.limit(100)                                   # first 100
>>> stations.limit(10, "rain_mm", ascending=False)        # 10 wettest

      merge()

      merge(other)
      Appends the features of another dataset (stacks the rows).

Columns missing on one side are left empty. The other dataset is
reprojected to this dataset's CRS.

Examples
--------
>>> both_years = vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer="2023").merge(vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer="2024"))

      join()

      join(other, on, right_on=None, how='inner')
      Joins the columns of another dataset or table by matching values in a column.

Each feature gets the columns of the matching row(s) of `other`.
Geometries come from this dataset; the other dataset's geometry is not
used. Columns with the same name get the suffix "_2".

Parameters
----------
other : Vector
    The dataset or table (CSV, Excel sheet, ...) to take columns from.
on : str
    Column of this dataset to match on.
right_on : str, optional
    Column of `other` to match on. Default: the same name as `on`.
how : "inner" or "left", default "inner"
    "inner" keeps only features with a match; "left" keeps all features
    (unmatched ones get empty values).

Returns
-------
Vector

Examples
--------
>>> population = vector.Open("survey.xlsx", layer="districts")      # a table
>>> stations.join(population, on="district").show(5)
>>> districts.join(population, on="name", right_on="district", how="left")

      spatialJoin()

      spatialJoin(other, predicate='intersects', how='inner')
      Joins the columns of another dataset by location.

Each feature gets the columns of the features of `other` it touches
(or lies within, contains, ...). A feature matching several features of
`other` appears once per match. `other` is reprojected to this
dataset's CRS. Columns with the same name get the suffix "_2".

Parameters
----------
other : Vector
    Dataset with geometries, e.g. district polygons.
predicate : str, default "intersects"
    "intersects", "within", "contains", "touches", "crosses",
    "overlaps", "covers" or "covered_by".
how : "inner" or "left", default "inner"
    "inner" keeps only features with a match; "left" keeps all.

Returns
-------
Vector

Examples
--------
>>> districts = vector.Open("districts.geojson")
>>> with_zone = stations.spatialJoin(districts)              # adds the polygon's columns
>>> stations.spatialJoin(districts, predicate="within", how="left")

      buffer()

      buffer(distance)
      Grows (or shrinks) every geometry by a distance in metres.

A point becomes a circle, a line a corridor, and a polygon gets wider.
Negative distances shrink polygons. Works in metres for
longitude/latitude data too (computed in a local UTM projection).

Parameters
----------
distance : float
    Distance in metres (CRS units for projected data, usually metres).

Returns
-------
Vector
    Same columns, buffered geometries, same CRS.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If the dataset has no geometries or no CRS.

Examples
--------
>>> circle = vector.Point(73.125, 33.700).buffer(500)       # 500 m radius
>>> corridor = roads.buffer(50)                              # 50 m each side
>>> inner = aoi.buffer(-100)                                 # 100 m inside the boundary

      cluster()

      cluster(clusterer, outputName='cluster', columns=None, region=None)
      Adds a column with each feature's cluster number.

Give a trained clusterer, or an untrained one to train it on this
dataset right away (on `columns`, default all numeric columns). Rows
with an empty value in any input column get an empty cluster.

Parameters
----------
clusterer : cluster.TrainedClusterer or cluster.Clusterer
    A trained clusterer (trained on columns with the same names), or an
    untrained one to train on this dataset.
outputName : str, default "cluster"
    Name of the new column.
columns : list of str, optional
    Columns to train on, when `clusterer` is not trained yet.
region : vector.Vector, optional
    When `clusterer` is not trained yet: train only on the features
    inside these shapes. All features still get a cluster.

Returns
-------
Vector

Raises
------
ValueError
    If a column the clusterer was trained on is missing.

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.kMeans(4, normalize=True).train(stations, inputProperties=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c"])
>>> grouped = stations.cluster(trained)
>>> grouped.visualize(column="cluster")
>>> stations.cluster(cluster.kMeans(4, normalize=True), columns=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c"])
>>> stations.cluster(cluster.kMeans(3), columns=["ndvi", "temp_c"], region=central)

      pca()

      pca(model, columns=None, standardize=False)
      Adds principal-component columns (PC1, PC2, ...) computed from numeric columns.

Give a trained PCA, or a number of components to train one on this
dataset right away (from `columns`, default all numeric columns).

Parameters
----------
model : pca.TrainedPCA, int or None
    A trained PCA, or the number of components to keep (None = all).
columns : list of str, optional
    Columns to train on, when `model` is a number.
standardize : bool, default False
    Scale columns to unit variance first, when `model` is a number.
    Recommended when columns have different units.

Returns
-------
Vector

Examples
--------
>>> with_pcs = stations.pca(2, columns=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "rain_mm", "temp_c"], standardize=True)
>>> with_pcs.show(5, columns=["station_id", "PC1", "PC2"])

      visualize()

      visualize(column=None, palette=None, color=None, edgecolor=None, linewidth=1.0, legend=True, save_chart=False, dpi=200)
      Draws the geometries as a map chart.

Polygons are drawn filled with an outline, lines as lines and points as
dots. Give a `column` to color the features by an attribute: numeric
columns get a palette and a colorbar, text columns one color per value
and a legend. The axes show map coordinates (longitude/latitude for
geographic CRSs). To draw a vector on top of an image, use
``img.visualize(overlay=vector)``.

Parameters
----------
column : str, optional
    Attribute column to color the features by.
palette : str or list of colors, optional
    Palette for `column`: a built-in palette, a matplotlib colormap or a
    list of colors (see raster.palettes()). Default: "viridis" for numbers,
    "tab10" for text.
color : str, optional
    Fill color when no `column` is given. Default: green.
edgecolor : str, optional
    Outline color. Default: dark green (white when coloring by `column`).
linewidth : float, default 1.0
    Outline / line width.
legend : bool, default True
    Show the colorbar or legend when `column` is given.
save_chart : bool, default False
    Also save the chart as "<file name>_<epoch time>.png" in the current folder.
dpi : int, default 200
    Resolution of the saved PNG.

Returns
-------
str or None
    The saved PNG file name when save_chart=True, otherwise None.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If the dataset has no geometries, or `column` doesn't exist.

Examples
--------
>>> aoi = vector.Open("boundary.shp")
>>> aoi.visualize()                                       # outlines and fill
>>> aoi.visualize(column="name")                          # one color per name
>>> vector.Open("stations.csv").visualize(column="rain_mm", palette="precipitation")
>>> aoi.visualize(color="none", edgecolor="red", save_chart=True)

      toGeoJSON()

      toGeoJSON()
      Returns the features as a GeoJSON dict (coordinates in EPSG:4326 longitude/latitude).

Examples
--------
>>> img.geometry().toGeoJSON()["features"][0]["geometry"]["coordinates"]

      save()

      save(path)
      Saves the dataset to a file; the format is chosen from the extension.

Supported: .geojson / .json, .shp, .gpkg, .kml, .parquet, .csv, .xlsx.
GeoJSON and KML are always written in EPSG:4326 (longitude/latitude), as
those formats require. In .csv and .xlsx, geometries are written as WKT
text in a "geometry" column.

Parameters
----------
path : str
    Output file.

Returns
-------
str
    The absolute path of the saved file.

Examples
--------
>>> img.geometry().save("extent.geojson")
>>> aoi.save("aoi.gpkg")

      Feature

      class Feature
      A single feature: a geometry plus a set of named properties.

Features are what `Vector.map()` passes to your function, and what
`Vector.get(i)` / `Vector.first()` return. Create one yourself with
``vector.Feature(geometry, {"name": value, ...})``. Features don't change:
`set()` returns a new feature.

Parameters
----------
geometry : shapely geometry, GeoJSON dict, or None
    The shape. None for a feature without geometry.
properties : dict, optional
    Property names and values.

Examples
--------
>>> from shapely.geometry import Point
>>> f = vector.Feature(Point(73.12, 33.70), {"name": "A", "rain_mm": 12.5})
>>> f.get("rain_mm")
12.5
>>> aoi.map(lambda f: vector.Feature(f.centroid(), {"name": f.get("name")}))   # polygons -> centre points

      get()

      get(name)
      Returns the value of one property.

Parameters
----------
name : str
    Property (column) name.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If the feature has no property with that name.

Examples
--------
>>> station = stations.first()
>>> station.get("rain_mm")
14.2
>>> stations.map(lambda f: f.set({"rain_cm": f.get("rain_mm") / 10}))

      set()

      set(*args)
      Returns a copy of the feature with properties added or changed.

Call it with a dict, ``set({"a": 1, "b": 2})``, or with one name and
value, ``set("a", 1)``. Existing properties with the same name are replaced.

Returns
-------
Feature

Examples
--------
>>> f.set({"rain_cm": f.get("rain_mm") / 10, "wet": f.get("rain_mm") > 20})
>>> f.set("checked", True)

Examples

>>> stations.first().properties()
{'station_id': 'ST0001', 'district': 'North', 'rain_mm': 14.2, ...}

>>> stations.first().propertyNames()
['station_id', 'name', 'district', ...]

>>> g.geom_type, g.bounds

      Filter

      class Filter
      A condition on feature properties, used with `Vector.filter()`.

Build filters with the static methods (``Filter.eq``, ``Filter.gt``, ...)
and combine them with ``&`` (and), ``|`` (or) and ``~`` (not), or with
``Filter.And`` / ``Filter.Or`` / ``Filter.Not``.

Examples
--------
>>> from earthforge.vector import Filter
>>> wet = stations.filter(Filter.gt("rain_mm", 20))
>>> north_forest = stations.filter(Filter.eq("district", "North") & Filter.eq("land_cover", "forest"))
>>> stations.filter(Filter.inList("district", ["North", "East"]) | ~Filter.notNull("rain_mm"))

      Keeps features whose property equals `value`.

Examples
--------
>>> stations.filter(Filter.eq("district", "North"))

Examples
--------

      Keeps features whose property is greater than `value`.

      Keeps features that pass ALL the filters. Operator form: ``a & b``.

      cluster

      Methods

      kMeans()

      cluster.kMeans(nClusters, maxIterations=300, restarts=4, normalize=False)
      Creates a k-means clusterer (scikit-learn's KMeans, k-means++ start).

Groups pixels or rows into `nClusters` clusters so that each is as close as
possible (Euclidean distance) to its cluster centre.

Parameters
----------
nClusters : int
    Number of clusters.
maxIterations : int, default 300
    Maximum iterations per run.
restarts : int, default 4
    Number of runs with different starts; the best is kept.
normalize : bool, default False
    Scale every input to 0-1 before clustering, so inputs with large
    values don't dominate.

Returns
-------
Clusterer

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)
>>> img.cluster(trained).visualize(palette="tab10", min=0, max=4)

      wekaKMeans()

      cluster.wekaKMeans(nClusters, init='random', distanceFunction='Euclidean', maxIterations=500, restarts=1, normalize=True)
      Creates a simple k-means clusterer in the style of Weka's SimpleKMeans.

Options for how the first centres are chosen and how distance is measured.
With Manhattan distance, cluster centres are medians instead of means.
Inputs are scaled to 0-1 by default, as in Weka.

Parameters
----------
nClusters : int
    Number of clusters.
init : str, default "random"
    How the first centres are picked: "random" (random samples),
    "kmeans++" (spread out by probability) or "farthestFirst" (each next
    centre is the sample farthest from those chosen so far).
distanceFunction : str, default "Euclidean"
    "Euclidean" or "Manhattan".
maxIterations : int, default 500
    Maximum iterations.
restarts : int, default 1
    Number of runs with different starts; the one with the lowest cost is kept.
normalize : bool, default True
    Scale every input to 0-1 before clustering.

Returns
-------
Clusterer

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)
>>> cluster.wekaKMeans(6, init="kmeans++", distanceFunction="Manhattan", restarts=5)

      wekaCascadeKMeans()

      cluster.wekaCascadeKMeans(minClusters=2, maxClusters=10, restarts=10, init='random', maxIterations=500, normalize=True)
      Creates a k-means clusterer that chooses the number of clusters itself.

Runs k-means for every number of clusters from `minClusters` to
`maxClusters` (each with several restarts) and keeps the number with the
best Calinski-Harabasz score (compact clusters that are far apart), in
the style of Weka's CascadeSimpleKMeans.

Parameters
----------
minClusters, maxClusters : int, default 2 and 10
    Range of cluster numbers to try.
restarts : int, default 10
    k-means runs per number of clusters; the best is kept.
init : str, default "random"
    "random", "kmeans++" or "farthestFirst" (see wekaKMeans).
maxIterations : int, default 500
    Maximum iterations per run.
normalize : bool, default True
    Scale every input to 0-1 before clustering.

Returns
-------
Clusterer

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.wekaCascadeKMeans(2, 8).train(img, numPixels=5000)
>>> trained.nClusters                      # the number it chose
>>> trained.info()                         # scores for every k

      wekaXMeans()

      cluster.wekaXMeans(minClusters=2, maxClusters=8, restarts=3, init='kmeans++', maxIterations=500, normalize=True)
      Creates a k-means clusterer that chooses the number of clusters by BIC.

Runs k-means for every number of clusters from `minClusters` to
`maxClusters` and keeps the one with the best Bayesian Information
Criterion, which rewards a good fit but penalizes extra clusters. Based on
the X-means idea (Pelleg and Moore), as in Weka's XMeans.

Parameters
----------
minClusters, maxClusters : int, default 2 and 8
    Range of cluster numbers to try.
restarts : int, default 3
    k-means runs per number of clusters; the best is kept.
init : str, default "kmeans++"
    "random", "kmeans++" or "farthestFirst".
maxIterations : int, default 500
    Maximum iterations per run.
normalize : bool, default True
    Scale every input to 0-1 before clustering.

Returns
-------
Clusterer

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.wekaXMeans(2, 10).train(img, numPixels=5000)
>>> trained.nClusters

      miniBatchKMeans()

      cluster.miniBatchKMeans(nClusters, batchSize=1024, maxIterations=100, normalize=False)
      Creates a mini-batch k-means clusterer: a faster k-means for large training samples.

Updates the centres from small random batches instead of all samples at
once; results are close to kMeans at a fraction of the time.

Parameters
----------
nClusters : int
    Number of clusters.
batchSize : int, default 1024
    Samples per batch.
maxIterations : int, default 100
    Maximum passes over the training data.
normalize : bool, default False
    Scale every input to 0-1 before clustering.

Returns
-------
Clusterer

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.miniBatchKMeans(6).train(img, numPixels=50000)

      bisectingKMeans()

      cluster.bisectingKMeans(nClusters, normalize=False)
      Creates a bisecting k-means clusterer.

Starts with one cluster and repeatedly splits the largest one in two.
Clusters tend to be more even in size than with plain k-means.

Parameters
----------
nClusters : int
    Number of clusters.
normalize : bool, default False
    Scale every input to 0-1 before clustering.

Returns
-------
Clusterer

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.bisectingKMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)

      gaussianMixture()

      cluster.gaussianMixture(nClusters, covariance='full', normalize=False)
      Creates a Gaussian mixture clusterer.

Models the data as a mix of `nClusters` Gaussian (bell-shaped) groups,
which can be stretched and tilted, so clusters don't have to be round.
Each pixel or row goes to its most likely group.

Parameters
----------
nClusters : int
    Number of clusters (Gaussian components).
covariance : str, default "full"
    Shape of each group: "full" (any shape), "diag" (axis-aligned),
    "spherical" (round) or "tied" (all the same shape).
normalize : bool, default False
    Scale every input to 0-1 before clustering.

Returns
-------
Clusterer

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.gaussianMixture(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)
>>> cluster.gaussianMixture(4, covariance="diag")

      Classes

      Clusterer

      class Clusterer
      A clustering method, ready to be trained. Create one with cluster.kMeans(), cluster.wekaKMeans(), ...

Examples
--------
>>> c = cluster.wekaKMeans(5)
>>> trained = c.train(img, numPixels=5000)

      train()

      train(data, inputProperties=None, numPixels=5000, seed=0, region=None)
      Trains the clusterer on an image sample or on a dataset's columns.

Parameters
----------
data : Image or Vector
    An Image: `numPixels` random pixels are sampled (reading only what
    is needed, so large images are fine) and all its bands are used.
    A Vector (e.g. ``img.sample()`` or a CSV): its numeric columns are used.
inputProperties : list of str, optional
    The bands / columns to use. Default: all bands, or all numeric columns.
numPixels : int, default 5000
    Pixels to sample when `data` is an Image.
seed : int, default 0
    Random seed, for the sample and the clustering (same seed = same result).
region : vector.Vector, optional
    Train only on pixels (or rows) inside these shapes.

Returns
-------
TrainedClusterer

Raises
------
ValueError
    If there are fewer valid samples than clusters, or a column is missing.

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(5).train(img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8"), numPixels=5000)
>>> trained = cluster.kMeans(4).train(stations, inputProperties=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "rain_mm"])
>>> trained = cluster.kMeans(5).train(img, region=vector.Open("boundary.shp"))

      TrainedClusterer

      class TrainedClusterer
      A trained clusterer: apply it with ``img.cluster(trained)`` or ``vector.cluster(trained)``.

Examples
--------
>>> trained = cluster.wekaKMeans(5).train(img, numPixels=5000)
>>> trained.info()
>>> clusters = img.cluster(trained)

      nClusters property

      The number of clusters (for cascade / X-means: the number chosen).

Examples
--------
>>> cluster.wekaCascadeKMeans(2, 8).train(img).nClusters
4

      schema()

      schema()
      Returns the names of the bands / columns the clusterer was trained on.

Images and tables you apply it to must have these bands / columns.

Examples
--------
>>> trained.schema()
['B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'B8']

      centers()

      centers()
      Returns the cluster centres, in the original units, as a table (one row per cluster).

For gaussianMixture these are the component means.

Examples
--------
>>> trained.centers()
        B2      B3      B4      B8
0    310.2   420.8   288.1  2650.4
...

      info()

      info()
      Prints a summary: method, settings, number of clusters, training size, cluster sizes and centres.

Returns
-------
dict
    method, params, nClusters, inputs, trainingSamples, clusterSizes, scores.

Examples
--------
>>> trained.info()

      pca

      PCA

      class PCA
      Principal component analysis, ready to be trained.

PCA turns many correlated bands (or columns) into a few uncorrelated
"principal components". PC1 holds the most variation, PC2 the most of what
is left, and so on, so the first few components usually summarize the data.

Parameters
----------
nComponents : int, optional
    Number of components to keep. Default: as many as there are inputs.
standardize : bool, default False
    Scale every input to unit variance first (correlation PCA). Use it
    when inputs have very different units or ranges, e.g. NDVI and
    elevation; leave it off for bands of one sensor.

Examples
--------
>>> model = pca.PCA(3).train(img, numPixels=10000)
>>> pcs = img.pca(model)
>>> pca.PCA(2, standardize=True).train(stations, inputProperties=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "temp_c"])

      train()

      train(data, inputProperties=None, numPixels=10000, seed=0, region=None)
      Learns the principal components from an image sample or a dataset's columns.

Parameters
----------
data : Image or Vector
    An Image: `numPixels` random pixels are sampled (reading only what
    is needed) and all its bands are used. A Vector: its numeric
    columns are used.
inputProperties : list of str, optional
    The bands / columns to use. Default: all bands, or all numeric columns.
numPixels : int, default 10000
    Pixels to sample when `data` is an Image.
seed : int, default 0
    Random seed for the sample.
region : vector.Vector, optional
    Learn only from pixels (or rows) inside these shapes, e.g. your
    study area. The components can then be applied to the whole image.

Returns
-------
TrainedPCA

Raises
------
ValueError
    If there are fewer valid samples than inputs, or nComponents is
    larger than the number of inputs.

Examples
--------
>>> model = pca.PCA(3).train(img.select("B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11", "B12"))
>>> model = pca.PCA().train(stations, inputProperties=["ndvi", "elevation_m", "rain_mm", "temp_c"])
>>> model = pca.PCA(3).train(img, region=vector.Open("boundary.shp"))      # only inside the boundary

      TrainedPCA

      class TrainedPCA
      A trained PCA: apply it with ``img.pca(model)`` or ``vector.pca(model)``.

Examples
--------
>>> model = pca.PCA(3).train(img)
>>> model.info()
>>> pcs = img.pca(model)

      nComponents property

      The number of components produced.

Examples
--------
>>> pca.PCA(3).train(img).nComponents
3

      schema()

      schema()
      Returns the names of the bands / columns the PCA was trained on.

Examples
--------
>>> model.schema()
['B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'B8', 'B11', 'B12']

      componentNames()

      componentNames()
      Returns the names of the output bands / columns: PC1, PC2, ...

Examples
--------
>>> model.componentNames()
['PC1', 'PC2', 'PC3']

      explainedVariance()

      explainedVariance()
      Returns the share of the total variance each kept component explains (0-1).

Examples
--------
>>> model.explainedVariance()
[0.912, 0.061, 0.018]
>>> sum(model.explainedVariance())          # share kept by all of them

      loadings()

      loadings()
      Returns how much each input contributes to each component, as a table.

Rows are inputs, columns are components. Large positive or negative
values mean the input drives that component.

Examples
--------
>>> model.loadings()
         PC1     PC2     PC3
B2     0.21   -0.44    0.10
...

      info()

      info()
      Prints the explained variance per component and the loadings.

Returns
-------
dict
    inputs, nComponents, standardize, trainingSamples, explainedVariance.

Examples
--------
>>> model.info()

      VectorNotFoundError

      class VectorNotFoundError(FileNotFoundError)
      Raised when the vector file does not exist.

      Raised when the file exists but cannot be read as a vector or table.

      Changelog

      All notable changes to this project are listed here. Versions follow __version__ in earthforge/__init__.py.

      [Unreleased]

      Nothing yet.

      [0.1.0] - 2026-11-25

      First public release, under the name EarthForge (pip install pyearthforge, then from earthforge import raster, vector, cluster, pca). The package was developed under the working name modules; the entries below list everything it contains.

      Packaging

      • Renamed the package from modules to earthforge. Imports change from from modules import ... to from earthforge import ..., and modules.FULL_TRACEBACKS becomes earthforge.FULL_TRACEBACKS.
      • Distribution name on PyPI: pyearthforge (the name earthforge is taken there). The import name stays earthforge.
      • pyproject.toml with all dependencies, extras [jupyter] (progress-bar widgets) and [docs] (documentation tools), MIT license, and built wheels.

      Added

      • Your own geometries: vector.Rectangle(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax), vector.Polygon([(x, y), ...]), vector.Point(x, y) and vector.fromGeometry(...) (GeoJSON geometry, Feature or FeatureCollection; WKT; shapely; several at once, with properties). All default to EPSG:4326 (lon/lat), and any CRS works. Use them as region= for sampling, PCA and clustering, or anywhere a vector is accepted.
      • Vector.buffer(metres) grows or shrinks geometries by a distance in metres, also for lon/lat data (e.g. a circle around a point).

      • PCA and Clustering docs: new "Sampling with your own geometry" sections.

      • One-step clustering with a region: img.cluster(cluster.kMeans(5), region=aoi, numPixels=..., seed=...) trains the clusterer on pixels inside the geometry and applies it, like img.pca(3, region=aoi). table.cluster(cluster.kMeans(4), columns=[...], region=aoi) does the same for tables. The result is identical to training and applying in two steps.

      • region= for sampling and training: img.sample(region=...), PCA.train(region=...), img.pca(n, region=...) and Clusterer.train(region=...) draw their pixels only inside a geometry, reprojected automatically. The full numPixels are drawn inside the region. For vector training data, region keeps the rows inside it.

      Changed

      • Sparse sampling: when samples are spread thinly over a large image, sample() (and so clustering/PCA training) reads only the small tiles that hold samples instead of whole blocks. Results are identical. On a 2.9 GB raster, 2,000 samples took 2.2 s and 1 MB instead of 3.1–5.6 s and about 110 MB. On a 200,000 × 200,000 mosaic it reads about 5,000 tiles instead of every block.

      • When blocks run in parallel, numpy and scikit-learn are limited to one thread per worker (threadpoolctl), so they don't compete with the workers for cores.

      • Clustering (from earthforge import cluster): kMeans, wekaKMeans (random, k-means++ or farthest-first start; Euclidean or Manhattan distance), wekaCascadeKMeans (chooses k by Calinski–Harabasz), wekaXMeans (chooses k by BIC), miniBatchKMeans, bisectingKMeans and gaussianMixture. Train with .train(img or vector), apply with img.cluster(trained) (lazy, saved as uint8) or vector.cluster(trained). TrainedClusterer has info(), centers(), schema() and nClusters.

      • PCA (from earthforge import pca): pca.PCA(nComponents, standardize).train(...), applied with img.pca(model) or vector.pca(model). Reports explainedVariance() and loadings(), and matches scikit-learn.
      • Image.sample(numPixels, seed) returns random pixels as a dataset, reading only the blocks that contain them.
      • Vector.columnNames() returns column names, like bandNames() for images.

      • Trained models are applied in chunks of 262,144 pixels, and the memory budget accounts for them: clustering an 8000 × 8000 × 4 raster peaks at 60 MB with one worker.

      • Records: Vector.show(n=10, columns=None) shows some or all records (show("all")). Vector.get(column) returns a column's values, and get(i) / first() return one Feature.

      • Filtering: Vector.filter(Filter...) with Filter.eq, neq, lt, lte, gt, gte, rangeContains, inList, stringContains, stringStartsWith, stringEndsWith, notNull, isNull, And, Or, Not, and the operators & | ~. Also filterBounds() (spatial), sort() and limit().
      • Custom columns: Vector.map(func), where the function returns f.set({...}) or vector.Feature(geometry, {...}), or None to drop the feature. Feature has get, set, properties, propertyNames, geometry, area (m², on the ellipsoid), length and centroid.
      • Joins: merge() appends features, join(other, on=...) matches on a column (also with tables), and spatialJoin(other, predicate=...) matches by location.

      • Sample data: sample_data/ holds 600 stations (CSV), a multi-sheet Excel survey and district polygons, generated reproducibly by sample_data/make_sample_data.py.

      • Vector.visualize() draws vectors as a map: polygons filled with outlines, lines and points. column= colors features by an attribute (numbers: palette and colorbar; text: legend).

      • Image.visualize(overlay=...) draws one or more vectors on top of an image, reprojected to the image's CRS. overlay_color sets one color or one per vector.

      • Parallel saving. save(workers=None) computes blocks in parallel threads (one per core, up to raster.MAX_WORKERS = 8), within a memory budget of about a quarter of the free RAM. The output is identical to one worker. Mosaics and calculations run about 2× faster on multi-core PCs.

      • Image.split(save=False) returns one single-band image per band. save=True or a folder path writes one GeoTIFF per band.
      • raster.stack(images, names=None) combines the bands of several images or files (a list, folder or pattern) into one image. Images on another grid are resampled onto the first image's grid. Repeated band names are prefixed with the file name.
      • raster.BLOCK_SIZE (default 1024) and raster.MAX_WORKERS (default 8) can be changed.
      • Every public function, method and property now has a description and a usage example, both in its docstring (shown by help() and in the API reference) and on its docs page. tools/check_docstrings.py checks this.

      Added (this release, earlier)

      • raster.mosaic(images, method="last", res=None) combines any number of rasters (a list, a folder or a glob pattern) without loading them. It works like a GDAL VRT: each saved block reads only the overlapping parts of the tiles. Methods: last, first, min, max, mean. Tiles may overlap, sit on different grids or have different resolutions. Computed images work too.
      • save() shows a progress bar (tqdm; a widget in Jupyter). Turn it off with progress=False.
      • save(dtype=..., nodata=...) chooses the file's data type and NoData value.
      • At most 64 source files are kept open at once, so mosaics of thousands of tiles work.

      Changed

      • save() writes 1024 × 1024 blocks instead of full-width strips, so memory stays small for very wide images. It is also faster: 3.2 s instead of 4.5 s for NDVI, and 6.4 s instead of 16 s for 4 bands, on an 8000 × 8000 raster.
      • save() keeps integer data types (e.g. uint16) when values pass through unchanged (select, clip, updateMask, first/last/min/max mosaics), instead of always writing float32. Computed results are still float32.

      Added (earlier)

      • vector module. vector.Open(path, layer=None, x=None, y=None, crs=None) reads Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML, KMZ, GeoPackage, Parquet/GeoParquet, CSV and Excel (any sheet). Tables become points (coordinate columns), shapes (WKT column) or plain tables. vector.layers(path) lists layers or sheets.
      • Vector.meta(), columns(), size(), hasGeometry(), geometryTypes(), toGeoJSON() and save(path) (.geojson, .shp, .gpkg, .kml, .parquet, .csv, .xlsx). The data, crs and bounds attributes.
      • Image.geometry() returns the image extent as a Vector, ready to print or export (e.g. .save("extent.geojson")).
      • Image.clip(vector) crops to the vector's bounding box and masks pixels outside the shapes. It reprojects automatically, and the result matches rasterio.mask.
      • Image.updateMask(mask) sets pixels to NoData where the mask is 0.
      • eq() / neq() accept a list of values, e.g. classified.eq([3, 4]).
      • Image.selectClasses(classes) keeps the listed classes; all others become NoData.
      • Image.mergeClasses(classes, into) or mergeClasses({new: [olds]}) merges classes.

      Changed

      • Image.bounds is now a method: bounds(save=False). It returns the same BoundingBox, and save=True (or a path) also writes the box as GeoJSON. Replace img.bounds.left with img.bounds().left.
      • FULL_TRACEBACKS moved to the package: import earthforge; earthforge.FULL_TRACEBACKS = True.

      Added (earlier)

      • Image.expression(expression, map) evaluates text formulas (also available as Image.Expression). Variables come from map, band names can be used directly, and b('name') / b(index) select bands. Supports + - * / **, comparisons, && || ! / and or not, and abs sqrt log log10 exp. Parsed safely with ast, never eval.
      • Image.where(*rules, otherwise=None) reclassifies a raster. It accepts a single where(test, value) rule or several rules given as tuples, a list, a dict or 2-item sets. Later rules win.
      • Comparisons lt, lte, gt, gte, eq, neq and logic And, Or, Not, with operators < <= > >= & | ~.
      • visualize(labels={value: "name"}) draws class maps with flat colors and a legend.
      • Using an Image as True/False (if img:, a and b) raises a TypeError that explains what to use instead.
      • Documentation website (MkDocs Material) with a home page, cheat sheet, and API reference generated from docstrings. New pages: Expressions, Reclassify.

      Fixed

      • visualize(bands=img.select("B8")) raised TypeError: object of type 'Image' has no len(). An Image passed as bands is now shown.

      • Image.remap(from_values, to_values=None, default=None) replaces exact values with new ones (lists or a {old: new} dict). Unlisted values are kept, or set to default. Values are matched against the original pixels, so mappings don't chain.

      • and_(), or_(), not_() as lowercase spellings of And(), Or(), Not().
      • raster.FULL_TRACEBACKS (default False) shows the library's internal frames when debugging.

      Changed

      • Short tracebacks. Errors raised by the library no longer show its internal frames (or unrelated source lines). In Jupyter / IPython only your code line and the message are shown. Errors are still normal ValueError / TypeError / RasterNotFoundError / RasterReadError instances.
      • "Band not found" message now reads Band 'B8' not found. This image has: ['B4'].
      • Docstrings rewritten with descriptive summary lines (for example "Calculates the Normalized Difference between two bands.") and Raises sections.
      • Error messages simplified, for example: 'palette' only works with a single band. Remove it or pass 1 band.

      Added (earlier in this release)

      • raster.image(path) opens a GeoTIFF as an Image.
      • Image.meta() prints and returns metadata, including band names.
      • Image.bandNames() returns a BandList: a list with .size() and .get(i).
      • Image.select(*bands) picks bands by name or 1-based number.
      • Image.rename(*names) and Image.addBands(other).
      • Band math: add, subtract, multiply, divide, pow (with an Image or a number), and abs, sqrt, log, log10, exp.
      • Operators + - * / **, unary - and abs(). Numbers work on either side.
      • Band pairing: same band count, or one single-band image applied to every band of the other.
      • Non-finite results (x/0, log(0), …) become NaN.
      • Image.normalizedDifference(bandNames) returns a single band named "nd".
      • save argument on every band-math method and on normalizedDifference: True for an automatic file name, or a path.
      • Image.save(path=None, compress="deflate") writes a float32 GeoTIFF in a streamed, tiled, multi-threaded way, with band names stored in the file.
      • Image.visualize() shows charts with bands, min, max, gamma and palette.
      • RGB composites (3 bands) and single-band views with a colorbar.
      • colorbar_label, colorbar_orientation ("vertical" / "horizontal"), max_size (preview resolution).
      • save_chart=True saves a PNG named <image>_<epoch>.png, at dpi=200 by default.
      • 16 built-in palettes (ndvi, ndwi, evi, ndbi, nbr, ndsi, elevation, temperature, precipitation, water, soil_moisture, night_lights, vegetation, diverging, change, blue_red), _r reversal, raster.palettes(), raster.showPalettes() and raster.PALETTES.
      • RasterNotFoundError and RasterReadError replace rasterio's long tracebacks.

      Changed (earlier in this release)

      • Images are now lazy. raster.image() reads only metadata. select() and band math build recipes. Pixels are read by visualize() (downsampled preview), save() (streamed) or .data.
      • Image.data is now computed on access as float32 (it was previously loaded in full at the file's dtype when the image was opened).

      Before 0.1.0 (working name modules)

      Added

      • add(a, b) and subtract(a, b).
